knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deterministic multiple-source river treatment optimization model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulation under linear mixing, complete mixing, deterministic reachwise propagation, and prescribed technological bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \begin{aligned}\min_{x}\quad &\sum_{i=1}^{I}C_i(x_i)\\ \text{s.t.}\quad &D_i^{\min}(x)\ge D_i^0,\quad i=1,\ldots,I,\\ &x_{i,\min}\le x_i\le x_{i,\max},\quad i=1,\ldots,I,\end{aligned}\qquad D_i^{\min}=D_i^s-D_i^c,\quad D_i^c=F_i(D_{0i},L_{0i},k_1,k_2),\quad L_{0i}=\frac{L_{ri}Q_{ri}+(1-x_i)L_iq_i}{Q_{ri}+q_i}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the treatment efficiencies at all discharge sites to minimize total treatment cost while ensuring that the minimum dissolved-oxygen level on every river reach meets its prescribed standard. Reachwise BOD levels are computed sequentially from linear complete-mixing balances and the deterministic oxygen-deficit model, subject to technological bounds on each treatment efficiency.
assumptions_latex: \text{linear load additivity, complete mixing, and deterministic sequential reach propagation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_x\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{I}C_i(x_i):D_i^{\min}(x)\ge D_i^0\ (i=1,\ldots,I),\ x_{i,\min}\le x_i\le x_{i,\max}\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition through one difference-of-convex inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(D\) is a d.c. set if there exists a d.c. function \(f\) such that \(D=\{x:f(x)\le 0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is a DC set if it is the nonpositive sublevel set of a difference-of-convex function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Union and Intersection Closure of DC Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure under any finite construction using unions and intersections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_1,\ldots,D_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be d.c. sets. Every set obtained from \(D_1,\ldots,D_k\) by finitely many union and intersection operations is a d.c. set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any set built from finitely many DC sets by finitely many unions and intersections is again a DC set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Online vertex enumeration after adding a cutting hyperplane
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Updates vertices and adjacency information after a polyhedral outer approximation is cut by l_k(x)=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize W=\varnothing. For each v\in V_k^+ and each adjacent u\in N(v)\cap V_k^-, find \lambda\in[0,1] satisfying l_k(\lambda v+(1-\lambda)u)=0 and create w=\lambda v+(1-\lambda)u. Replace the crossing adjacency at u by w, initialize the new vertex's adjacency and active-index set using the common active indices of u and v together with the new constraint index, and add w to W. Finally, for u,v\in W, declare them adjacent whenever |I(u)\cap I(v)|=n-1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every edge crossing the new hyperplane, compute its intersection point, replace the discarded endpoint in the retained endpoint's neighbor data, record the new constraint and inherited active constraints, and then connect pairs of new vertices sharing n−1 active constraints.
assumptions_latex: P_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is represented by vertices, neighbor sets }N(\cdot),\text{ and active-index sets }I(\cdot)
V_k^+\text{ and }V_k^-\text{ are the vertices on opposite sides of }l_k(x)=0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W\text{ and the updated }N(\cdot),I(\cdot)\text{ enumerate the new cut-boundary vertices and their adjacencies}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-Union Constructions of DC Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient geometric constructions for a set to admit a DC-inequality representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\ge 1\). Every finite union of closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^m\) is a d.c. set. Also, if \(U_1,\ldots,U_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) are open and convex, then \(\mathbb{R}^m\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^k U_i\) is a d.c. set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite union of closed convex sets is a DC set, and so is the complement in Euclidean space of a finite union of open convex sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigcup_{i=1}^k C_i\text{ and }\mathbb{R}^m\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^{\ell}U_j\text{ are d.c. sets}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise definition of a vector-valued DC mapping on a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(F=(f_1,\ldots,f_m):\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^m\). Then \(F\in DC(\Omega)\) if and only if \(f_i\in DC(\Omega)\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector-valued mapping on a convex set is DC exactly when each component function is DC.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\in DC(\Omega)\iff \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,m\},\ f_i\in DC(\Omega)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Difference-of-Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a DC function on a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. A function \(f:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) is DC on \(\Omega\) if there exist convex functions \(p,q:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) such that \(f(x)=p(x)-q(x)\) for all \(x\in\Omega\). The set of such functions is denoted \(DC(\Omega)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued function on a convex set is DC if it is the difference of two convex functions on that set; their class is denoted DC(Omega).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in DC(\Omega)\iff \exists\,p,q:\Omega\to\mathbb R\text{ convex with }f=p-q

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Linear and Lattice Closure of DC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of DC functions under finite real linear combinations, pointwise maxima, and pointwise minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(f_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be DC functions on \(\Omega\). For arbitrary \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m\in\mathbb{R}\), the functions \(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f_i\), \(\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i\), and \(\min_{1\le i\le m}f_i\) are DC on \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a common convex domain, every finite real linear combination, pointwise maximum, and pointwise minimum of DC functions is again DC.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f_i,\quad \max_{1\le i\le m}f_i,\quad \min_{1\le i\le m}f_i\text{ are DC on }\Omega

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC representations of maxisum and minisum facility objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Difference-of-convex decompositions for continuous single-facility objectives with attractive and repulsive users.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J_1,J_2\) index attraction and repulsion points, and let \(h_j:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R_+\) be convex with \(h_j(x)\to+\infty\) as \(\|x\|\to\infty\). For the maxisum objective \(F(x)=\sum_{j\in J_1}q_j(h_j(x))-\sum_{j\in J_2}q_j(h_j(x))\), suppose each \(q_j:\mathbb R_+\to\mathbb R_+\) is convex and decreasing and \(q'_{j,+}(0)>-\infty\). If \(K_j\geq |q'_{j,+}(0)|\) and \(g_j=q_j\circ h_j+K_jh_j\), then \(g_j\) is convex and \(F=G-H\), where \(G=\sum_{j\in J_1}g_j+\sum_{j\in J_2}K_jh_j\) and \(H=\sum_{j\in J_2}g_j+\sum_{j\in J_1}K_jh_j\). Analogously, when the signed objective is minimized, each \(q_j\) is concave and increasing, and \(q'_{j,+}(0)<+\infty\), it has a DC representation with \(G=\sum_{j\in J_2}g_j+\sum_{j\in J_1}K_jh_j\) and \(H=\sum_{j\in J_1}g_j+\sum_{j\in J_2}K_jh_j\), where the analogous transformation produces convex \(g_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated convexity or concavity and finite right-slope assumptions, signed sums of distance-dependent attraction or cost terms admit explicit difference-of-convex representations. Negating the objective converts maxisum and minisum formulations into one another.
assumptions_latex: h_j:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R_+\text{ is convex and }h_j(x)\to+\infty\text{ as }\|x\|\to\infty
\text{Maxisum: }q_j:\mathbb R_+\to\mathbb R_+\text{ is convex and decreasing, with }q'_{j,+}(0)>-\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(x)=G(x)-H(x)\quad\text{for convex }G,H.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC structure of multifacility objectives with pairwise interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous multifacility location objectives combining facility-user costs with pairwise facility-interaction costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let r\ge 2 and X=(x^1,\ldots,x^r)\in(\mathbb R^2)^r. Suppose each F_i(x^i) is d.c., each h_{il}(x^i,x^l) is convex and nonnegative, and each \rho_{il}:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R is concave and increasing with finite right derivative at 0. Then \Phi(X)=\sum_{i=1}^r F_i(x^i)+\sum_{i<l}\rho_{il}(h_{il}(x^i,x^l)) is d.c. on (\mathbb R^2)^r. Under the preceding assumptions, if every F_i is convex and every \rho_{il} is also convex, then \Phi is convex. If \rho_{il}\equiv0 for every i<l, minimizing \Phi separates into r independent single-facility minisum problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous multifacility objective consisting of DC facility-user costs and concave increasing transformations of nonnegative convex pairwise interaction measures is DC. It is convex in the stated convex special case and separates into independent single-facility problems when all pairwise interactions vanish.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi\text{ is d.c. on }(\mathbb R^2)^r;\quad [F_i\text{ convex and }\rho_{il}\text{ convex for all }i<l]\Rightarrow\Phi\text{ convex};\quad [\rho_{il}\equiv0\ \forall i<l]\Rightarrow\min\Phi\text{ separates into }r\text{ independent problems}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC representation of lower-semicontinuous inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a lower-semicontinuous zero-sublevel condition using the fixed quadratic convex component $\lVert x\rVert^2$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every lower-semicontinuous function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$, there exists a convex function $g$ such that, for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, $f(x)\le0$ if and only if $g(x)-\lVert x\rVert^2\le0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every lower-semicontinuous zero-sublevel inequality is equivalent to a DC inequality whose subtracted convex term is the squared Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists g\text{ convex such that }\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\quad f(x)\le0\iff g(x)-\lVert x\rVert^2\le0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Density of DC Functions on Compact Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform approximation of continuous real-valued functions by difference-of-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be compact and convex. For every continuous function \(f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists a d.c. function \(g\) on \(\Omega\) such that \(|f(x)-g(x)|\leq\varepsilon\) for all \(x\in\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every continuous real-valued function on a compact convex set can be uniformly approximated to arbitrary accuracy by a DC function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists g\text{ d.c. on }\Omega\text{ such that }\forall x\in\Omega,\ |f(x)-g(x)|\leq\varepsilon\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Locally DC Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local difference-of-convex representability around every point of a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\). The function \(f\) is locally DC if, for every \(x\in D\), there exist a convex open neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\) and convex functions \(g,h:U\to\mathbb{R}\) such that \(f(y)=g(y)-h(y)\) for every \(y\in D\cap U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function on a convex set is locally DC if every point has a convex open neighborhood on which the function, wherever defined, agrees with the difference of two convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is locally DC}\iff \forall x\in D\;\exists U,g,h\;\forall y\in D\cap U:\ f(y)=g(y)-h(y)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Representation under Convex Nondecreasing Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A constructive DC decomposition for a bounded nonnegative DC argument, with monomial and signomial consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be compact and convex, let \(u,v:\Omega\to\mathbb R_+\) be convex, and set \(h=u-v\) with \(0\le h(x)\le a\) for every \(x\in\Omega\). If \(q:[0,a]\to\mathbb R\) is convex and nondecreasing with \(q'_-(a)<\infty\), then, for every \(K\ge q'_-(a)\), the function \(G(x)=q(h(x))+K[a+v(x)-u(x)]\) is convex and \(q(h(x))=G(x)-K[a+v(x)-u(x)]\); hence \(q\circ h\in DC(\Omega)\). Consequently, for \(\alpha\in\mathbb R_+^n\), the monomial \(x^\alpha\) is DC on every box \([r,s]\subset\mathbb R_{++}^n\), and every finite signomial \(\sum_\alpha c_\alpha x^\alpha\), with \(c_\alpha\in\mathbb R\), is DC there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex nondecreasing function composed with a bounded, nonnegative DC function has an explicit DC decomposition when its left derivative at the upper endpoint is finite. This makes nonnegative-real-exponent monomials, and finite real linear combinations of them, DC on positive boxes.
assumptions_latex: q:[0,a]\to\mathbb R\text{ is convex and nondecreasing}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q\circ h\in DC(\Omega),\qquad q(h)=G-K(a+v-u),\quad G=q(h)+K(a+v-u)\text{ convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Undominated DC Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional DC decompositions ordered by removal of a common convex component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A DC decomposition \(f=g-h\) is undominated if there are no other convex functions \(\bar g,\bar h\) forming a DC decomposition \(f=\bar g-\bar h\) and no nonconstant convex function \(p\) such that \(g=\bar g+p\) and \(h=\bar h+p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DC decomposition is undominated if no nonconstant convex term can be removed from both convex components while preserving a decomposition of the same function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists\,(\bar g,\bar h,p):\ f=\bar g-\bar h,\ p\text{ nonconstant and convex},\ g=\bar g+p,\ h=\bar h+p

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded-Variation Characterization of Univariate DC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization on [0,a], including finiteness of the indicated one-sided endpoint derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function f:[0,a]\to\mathbb{R} admits a representation f=p-q with convex p,q:[0,a]\to\mathbb{R} and finite p'_+(0),p'_-(a),q'_+(0),q'_-(a) if and only if there exists a bounded-variation function r:[0,a]\to\mathbb{R} such that f(x)=f(0)+\int_0^x r(t)\,dt for every x\in[0,a].
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A univariate function on [0,a] has a DC decomposition whose convex components have finite indicated endpoint one-sided derivatives exactly when it is the integral of a bounded-variation function, up to its value at zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\exists\text{ convex }p,q:\ f=p-q,\ p'_+(0),p'_-(a),q'_+(0),q'_-(a)\in\mathbb{R}\bigr]\iff\bigl[\exists r\in BV([0,a]):\ \forall x\in[0,a],\ f(x)=f(0)+\int_0^x r(t)\,dt\bigr]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Representation after a Convex Nonincreasing Outer Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit d.c. representation when the nonnegative inner function is itself expressed as a difference of two nonnegative convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) be compact and convex, and let \(u,v:M\to\mathbb{R}_+\) be convex with \(\widetilde h=u-v\ge0\) on \(M\). Let \(q:\mathbb{R}_+\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and nonincreasing with \(q^+(0)>-\infty\). If \(K\ge |q^+(0)|\), then \[q(\widetilde h(x))=g(x)-K(u(x)+v(x)),\] where \(g(x)=q(\widetilde h(x))+K(u(x)+v(x))\) is convex on \(M\). Consequently, \(q\circ\widetilde h\) is d.c. on \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a nonnegative difference of two nonnegative convex functions is composed with a convex nonincreasing function having a finite right derivative at zero, the composition is difference-of-convex. The decomposition uses a sufficiently large multiple of the sum of the two convex components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g:=q\circ\widetilde h+K(u+v)\text{ is convex on }M\text{ and }q\circ\widetilde h=g-K(u+v)\text{ is d.c. on }M

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extracted Closed-Ball Definition of a Locally DC Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract explicitly permits radius zero; this makes the condition degenerate unless a positive-radius requirement is imposed elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n and \epsilon\ge 0, let B(x_0,\epsilon)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\|x-x_0\|\le\epsilon\}. A function f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} is locally DC in the extracted sense if, for every x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n, there exists \epsilon\ge 0 such that f|_{B(x_0,\epsilon)} is DC.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the extracted definition, every point must have a closed ball on which the function is DC, but the permitted zero radius creates a degenerate boundary case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is locally DC in the extracted sense}\iff \forall x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\;\exists\epsilon\ge0:\ f|_{B(x_0,\epsilon)}\text{ is DC}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-set representation by affine-minus-strictly-convex inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to every closed subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space and every fixed real-valued strictly convex function on that space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be strictly convex and let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed. For every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus S\), there exists an affine function \(\ell:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\ell(y)-h(y)>0\) and \(\ell(x)-h(x)\le 0\) for all \(x\in S\). Moreover, there exists a countable family of affine functions \((\ell_i)_{i\ge1}\) such that \[S=\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ell_i(x)-h(x)\le0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given any real-valued strictly convex function on Euclidean space, every point outside a closed set can be strictly separated from it by an affine-minus-convex inequality. The closed set is the intersection of countably many sets defined by such inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus S\;\exists\ell\text{ affine}:\ \ell(y)-h(y)>0\ \land\ \forall x\in S,\ \ell(x)-h(x)\le0,\quad\text{and}\quad \exists(\ell_i)_{i\ge1}\text{ affine}:\ S=\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ell_i(x)-h(x)\le0\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure and Finite-Constraint Aggregation for DC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-lattice closure and its finite conjunctive and disjunctive encoding consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(f_i\in DC(\Omega)\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\). For arbitrary \(\alpha_i\in\mathbb R\), the functions \(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f_i\), \(\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i\), and \(\min_{1\le i\le m}f_i\) belong to \(DC(\Omega)\). Consequently, \(|f|\in DC(\Omega)\) for \(f\in DC(\Omega)\), and \(gh\in DC(\Omega)\) for \(g,h\in DC(\Omega)\). Moreover, \(g_i(x)\le0\) for every \(i\) is equivalent to \(\max_i g_i(x)\le0\), whereas \(g_i(x)\le0\) for at least one \(i\) is equivalent to \(\min_i g_i(x)\le0\). Thus any finite conjunctive or disjunctive system of DC inequalities can be rewritten as one DC inequality, and a DC optimization problem can be reduced to the canonical form \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(g(x)\le0\le h(x)\), where \(f,g,h\) are convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DC functions are closed under finite linear combinations, pointwise maxima and minima, absolute values, and products. Maxima encode conjunctions of DC inequalities and minima encode disjunctions, leading to a single-inequality encoding and the stated canonical DC program form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_i\alpha_i f_i,\ \max_i f_i,\ \min_i f_i\in DC(\Omega),\quad \bigwedge_i[g_i\le0]\iff \max_i g_i\le0,\quad \bigvee_i[g_i\le0]\iff \min_i g_i\le0

knowledge_statements.title: Basic Composite DC Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite maxima and minima of real-valued DC functions on a common convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(f_i=g_i-h_i\) on \(C\), where \(g_i,h_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). With \(H=\sum_{j=1}^m h_j\), one has
\[
\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i=\max_{1\le i\le m}\left(g_i+\sum_{j\ne i}h_j\right)-H.
\]
The maximum on the right is convex, so the displayed formula is a DC representation. Moreover,
\[
\min_{1\le i\le m}f_i=-\max_{1\le i\le m}(-f_i),
\]
and therefore every finite minimum is also DC.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite maxima and minima of DC functions are DC, with an explicit decomposition obtained by collecting all convex negative components.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i\) and \(h_i\) are finite convex functions on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_i f_i\) and \(\min_i f_i\) admit explicit DC representations on \(C\).

notation.meaning: DC decomposition of the ith function

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vector-Space Closure of DC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite linear combinations of real-valued DC functions on a common convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and \(f_i=g_i-h_i\), where \(g_i,h_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex. For \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}\), write \(a_i^+=\max\{a_i,0\}\) and \(a_i^-=\max\{-a_i,0\}\). Then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m a_i f_i=
\left(\sum_i a_i^+g_i+\sum_i a_i^-h_i\right)-
\left(\sum_i a_i^+h_i+\sum_i a_i^-g_i\right),
\]
so every finite real linear combination is DC on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite real linear combinations of DC functions are DC, with negative coefficients exchanging the two convex components.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) has a finite convex-minus-convex representation on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i=1}^m a_i f_i\) is DC on \(C\).

notation.meaning: positive and negative parts of the coefficient

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Products of DC Functions on Compact Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive product closure for finite DC functions on a compact convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(f=g-h\) and \(u=v-w\) with finite convex components. Choose constants so that \(G=g+a\), \(H=h+a\), \(V=v+b\), and \(W=w+b\) are nonnegative on \(K\). For nonnegative convex \(r,s\),
\[
rs=\tfrac12(r+s)^2-\tfrac12r^2-\tfrac12s^2
\]
is a DC representation. Hence
\[
fu=GV+HW-GW-HV
\]
admits a DC decomposition on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise product of two finite DC functions on a compact convex set is DC; nonnegative shifts of their convex components yield an explicit construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((g-h)(v-w)\) is DC on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.title: Products of DC Functions on Compact Convex Sets

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC representation for a convex nondecreasing function of a bounded DC function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite DC representation using the upper bound of the inner function and the left derivative of the outer function at that endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) be compact and convex, let \(u,v:M\to\mathbb{R}_+\) be convex, and set \(h=u-v\). Suppose \(0\le h(x)\le a\) for every \(x\in M\). Let \(q:[0,a]\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and nondecreasing with \(q'_-(a)<+\infty\). For every constant \(K\ge q'_-(a)\), \[g(x):=q(h(x))+K(a+v(x)-u(x))\] is convex on \(M\), and \[q(h(x))=g(x)-K(a+v(x)-u(x))\] is a DC representation on \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let h=u-v take values in [0,a] on a compact convex set, where u and v are nonnegative convex functions. If q is convex and nondecreasing on [0,a] with finite left derivative at a, then for every K at least that derivative, q(h)+K(a+v-u) is convex. Hence q(h) is DC with convex components g and K(a+v-u).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g:=q\circ h+K(a+v-u)\text{ is convex on }M,\qquad q\circ h=g-K(a+v-u)\text{ is DC on }M.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex nonincreasing composition with a nonnegative DC function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition rule for a nonnegative DC inner function represented as the difference of two nonnegative convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) be compact and convex, let \(u,v:M\to\mathbb{R}_+\) be convex, and set \(h=u-v\), where \(h(x)\ge0\) for all \(x\in M\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let h=u-v be nonnegative on a compact convex set, with u and v nonnegative and convex. knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g:=q\circ h+K(u+v)\text{ is convex on }M,\qquad q\circ h=g-K(u+v)\text{ is DC on }M.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concave Nondecreasing Composition of a Nonnegative DC Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient DC representation for a concave nondecreasing scalar composition under nonnegativity and finite-right-derivative assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) be compact and convex, let \(u,v:M\to\mathbb{R}_+\) be convex, and define \(\widetilde h=u-v\), where \(\widetilde h(x)\ge 0\) for all \(x\in M\). Let \(q:\mathbb{R}_+\to\mathbb{R}\) be concave and nondecreasing with \(q^+(0)<\infty\). If \(K\ge |q^+(0)|\), then \[q(\widetilde h(x))=K(u(x)+v(x))-g(x),\qquad g(x)=K(u(x)+v(x))-q(\widetilde h(x)),\] and \(g\) is convex on \(M\). Consequently, \(q\circ\widetilde h\) is a DC function on \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact convex set, let a nonnegative function be represented as the difference of two nonnegative convex functions. If a concave nondecreasing scalar function has finite right derivative at zero, then its composition with that DC function is DC. For any constant K at least the absolute value of that derivative, the stated remainder g is convex and supplies the DC decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g=K(u+v)-q\circ\widetilde h\text{ is convex on }M,\qquad q\circ\widetilde h=K(u+v)-g\text{ is DC on }M

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral-Shift DC Representation of an Indefinite Quadratic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The spectral-radius bound is sufficient for convexity but may be more conservative than the exact shift threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be symmetric and indefinite, let f(x)=x^TQx, and let \rho(Q) be the spectral radius of Q. knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(x)=f(x)+\lambda\|x\|^2\text{ is convex},\qquad f(x)=g(x)-\lambda\|x\|^2\text{ is DC}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Representation of a Continuous Piecewise-Linear Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive univariate representation using convex functions associated with concave breakpoints.

knowledge_statements.title: Separable DC Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additively separable functions whose univariate or block components have DC decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_m\), where each \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) is convex. Suppose \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is separable,
\[
f(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=c+\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i),
\]
and each component satisfies \(f_i=g_i-h_i\) with convex \(g_i,h_i:C_i\to\mathbb{R}\). Then
\[
f(x)=\left(c+\sum_{i=1}^m g_i(x_i)\right)-\sum_{i=1}^m h_i(x_i),
\]
where both displayed aggregate functions are convex on \(C\). Thus componentwise DC decompositions combine directly into a DC decomposition of the separable function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite sum of separable DC components is DC; summing their positive and negative convex parts gives the decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=\left(c+\sum_i g_i\right)-\sum_i h_i\) is DC on \(C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial DC Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic convexification of a polynomial restricted to a compact convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(p:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be a polynomial. Choose
\[
\rho\ge \max_{x\in K}\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2p(x))\}.
\]
Define \(g(x)=p(x)+(\rho/2)\lVert x\rVert_2^2\) and \(h(x)=(\rho/2)\lVert x\rVert_2^2\). Then \(\nabla^2g(x)=\nabla^2p(x)+\rho I\succeq0\) on \(K\), so \(g\) and \(h\) are convex on \(K\), and
\[
p=g-h\quad\text{on }K.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every polynomial restricted to a compact convex set has a DC decomposition obtained by adding and subtracting a sufficiently large quadratic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=g-h\) on \(K\), with \(g\) and \(h\) convex on \(K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Fixed Quadratic Need Not Convexify a Polynomial Globally
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the compact-set quadratic convexification construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(p(x)=-x^4\) and any \(\rho\ge0\),
\[
\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\left(p(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}x^2\right)=-12x^2+\rho,
\]
which is negative for sufficiently large \(|x|\). Thus no fixed quadratic shift makes this polynomial convex on all of \(\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact-domain quadratic convexification does not extend unchanged to the whole space: negative quartic curvature eventually dominates every fixed quadratic shift.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p+(\rho/2)x^2\) is not globally convex for any finite \(\rho\).
knowledge_statements.title: A Fixed Quadratic Need Not Convexify a Polynomial Globally

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global DC Decomposition of Every Polynomial
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Whole-space polynomial DC representation using a higher-degree radial convexifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). Choose an integer \(d\ge1\) with \(2d>\deg p\), and set \(q_d(x)=(1+\lVert x\rVert_2^2)^d\). There exists \(\rho\ge0\) such that
\[
\nabla^2p(x)+\rho\nabla^2q_d(x)\succeq0\quad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Consequently,
\[
p=(p+\rho q_d)-\rho q_d
\]
is a difference of two globally convex polynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every real polynomial is globally DC after adding and subtracting a sufficiently large higher-degree radial convex polynomial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is the difference of two polynomials convex on all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Global DC Decomposition of Every Polynomial

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity and Boundary Extrema of Quadratic Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines a whole-space boundedness criterion with the location of extrema of indefinite quadratics on compact convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be quadratic. If \(q\) is bounded below on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(q\) is convex. If \(q\) is indefinite and \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex, then both the minimum and the maximum of \(q\) on \(C\) are attained at boundary points of \(C\); such points need not be extreme points of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic bounded below on all of Euclidean space is convex. On a nonempty compact convex set, an indefinite quadratic attains its minimum and maximum on the boundary, though not necessarily at extreme points.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the second conclusion, }q\text{ is indefinite and }\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is compact and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q\text{ bounded below on }\mathbb{R}^n\Rightarrow q\text{ convex};\qquad \operatorname{argmin}_{C}q\cap\partial C\ne\varnothing,\quad \operatorname{argmax}_{C}q\cap\partial C\ne\varnothing

knowledge_statements.title: Universality of DC Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth universality on compact convex domains, not an unrestricted representation of arbitrary continuous functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and suppose \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(K\). Continuity of \(\nabla^2f\) gives a finite \(\rho\ge0\) such that \(\nabla^2f(x)+\rho I\succeq0\) for every \(x\in K\). Consequently,
\[
f(x)=\left(f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert x\rVert_2^2\right)-\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert x\rVert_2^2,
\]
and both terms in parentheses are convex on \(K\). Hence every such smooth function is DC on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every twice continuously differentiable function on a neighborhood of a compact convex set is DC on that set.
assumptions_latex: \(f\in C^2(U)\) for some open set \(U\supseteq K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is representable as a difference of two convex functions on \(K\).

notation.meaning: open neighborhood of the compact domain

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Unrestricted Continuous and C1 Universality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional boundary showing that DC universality does not extend to arbitrary continuous or continuously differentiable functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A differentiable function on a compact interval is DC only if its derivative has bounded variation. Consequently, if \(w:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous with unbounded total variation and
\[
f(x)=\int_0^x w(t)\,dt,
\]
then \(f\in C^1([0,1])\) but \(f\) is not DC on \([0,1]\). In particular, neither continuity nor continuous differentiability alone guarantees a DC representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A C1 function whose derivative has unbounded variation is not DC, so unrestricted C0 or C1 universality is false.
assumptions_latex: \(w:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous and has unbounded total variation.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Unrestricted Continuous and C1 Universality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz-Gradient DC Universality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic DC representation under a uniform first-order smoothness bound on a convex neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and convex, and let \(f\in C^1(U)\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Then \(x\mapsto f(x)+\frac{L}{2}\lVert x\rVert_2^2\) is convex on \(U\), and
\[
f(x)=\left(f(x)+\frac{L}{2}\lVert x\rVert_2^2\right)-\frac{L}{2}\lVert x\rVert_2^2
\]
is a DC representation on \(U\) and on every convex subset of \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuously differentiable function with Lipschitz gradient is DC after adding and subtracting a quadratic of matching curvature.
assumptions_latex: \(\lVert\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\rVert_2\le L\lVert x-y\rVert_2\) for all \(x,y\in U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is DC on \(U\).
knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz-Gradient DC Universality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Function in the Universal Closed-Set DC Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the supremum construction later used to represent an arbitrary closed set by a DC inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed, let \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be strictly convex, and let \(d\) be its associated set-separation functional. Choose \(\theta>0\) and \(r:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R_+\) such that \(r(x)=0\) for every \(x\in S\) and \(0<r(y)\leq\min\{\theta,d(y)\}\) for every \(y\notin S\). Define
\[
g_S(x)=\sup_{\substack{y\notin S\\p\in\partial h(y)}}\left\{h(y)+\langle p,x-y\rangle+r^2(y)\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given the separation functional, choose a nonnegative function r that vanishes on S and is positive but bounded by both theta and d outside S. The function g_S is the supremum of shifted supporting affine functions of h based at points outside S.
assumptions_latex: S\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and closed}
h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\text{ is strictly convex}
d\text{ is the associated set-separation functional}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g_S(x)=\sup_{y\notin S,\,p\in\partial h(y)}\left\{h(y)+\langle p,x-y\rangle+r^2(y)\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure of DC Functions under Smooth Composition, Products, Reciprocals, and Roots
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The composition result retains the domain hypotheses incorporated by reference from Proposition 4.4; the remaining conclusions are the corollary's stated special cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\) be as in Proposition 4.4. If \(F_1:\Omega_1\to\Omega_2\) is DC on \(\Omega_1\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(F_2:\Omega_2\to\mathbb{R}^k\) is \(C^2\)-smooth, then \(F_2\circ F_1\) is DC on \(\Omega_1\). In particular, the product of two DC functions is DC. If \(f\) is DC on an open or closed convex set \(\Omega\) and \(f(x)\neq0\) for every \(x\in\Omega\), then \(1/f\) and \(|f|^{1/m}\) are DC on \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subject to the domain hypotheses referenced in Proposition 4.4, composing a DC mapping with a twice continuously differentiable outer mapping preserves the DC property. Products of DC functions are DC. A nowhere-zero DC function on an open or closed convex set has both a DC reciprocal and a DC absolute-value m-th root.
assumptions_latex: \(f\text{ is DC on an open or closed convex set }\Omega\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_2\circ F_1\text{ is DC on }\Omega_1;\text{ products of DC functions are DC; and }1/f\text{ and }|f|^{1/m}\text{ are DC on }\Omega\text{ under the stated assumptions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Universality Properties of DC Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DC representability of smooth functions, density among continuous functions, and DC-inequality representation of closed sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is compact and convex, every \(C^2\) function on \(\Omega\) is DC on \(\Omega\). Consequently, every polynomial is DC on \(\Omega\), and \(DC(\Omega)\) is dense in \(C(\Omega)\) in the supremum norm. Separately, if \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is closed and \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is strictly convex, then there exists a continuous convex function \(g_S:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) such that \(S=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_S(x)-h(x)\le0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every twice continuously differentiable function is DC on a compact convex set; hence polynomials are DC and DC functions are uniformly dense among continuous functions there. Every closed Euclidean set also admits a representation by one DC inequality with any prescribed strictly convex subtractive term.
assumptions_latex: h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\text{ is strictly convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in DC(\Omega),\quad \overline{DC(\Omega)}^{\|\cdot\|_\infty}=C(\Omega),\quad \exists\,g_S\text{ continuous and convex}:S=\{x:g_S(x)-h(x)\le0\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Representation Does Not Imply Convexity or Connectedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary intrinsic boundary for the geometry of a set represented by one DC inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(C=\mathbb{R}\), the DC inequality
\[
1-x^2\le0
\]
represents
\[
D=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty).
\]
Here \(1-x^2=1-(x^2)\) is a difference of finite convex functions, while \(D\) is neither convex nor connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even one DC inequality can represent a disconnected, nonconvex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\) is DC-represented but neither convex nor connected.
knowledge_statements.title: DC Representation Does Not Imply Convexity or Connectedness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite DC-Inequality Set Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational finite-inequality convention for DC-represented sets relative to a convex ambient domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex. A finite DC-inequality representation of \(D\subseteq C\) is
\[
D=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x\in C:g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le0\},
\]
where \(m\) is finite and every \(g_i,h_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite and convex. The designation concerns the representation, not convexity of \(D\), and the same set may admit many such representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finitely DC-represented set is an intersection of finitely many DC sublevel regions inside a convex ambient domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed family is a finite DC-inequality representation of \(D\) relative to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite DC-Inequality Set Representation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-Inequality Normal Form and Finite Set Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal form and finite union/intersection closure for the explicitly scoped DC-inequality-represented class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If
\[
D=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x\in C:f_i(x)\le0\}
\]
with finite DC functions \(f_i\), then
\[
D=\{x\in C:\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\le0\},
\]
and the finite maximum is DC. Consequently, finite intersections of finitely DC-represented sets remain finitely DC-represented. Finite unions do as well: after writing \(D_j=\{x:F_j(x)\le0\}\),
\[
\bigcup_{j=1}^rD_j=\{x\in C:\min_{1\le j\le r}F_j(x)\le0\},
\]
and the finite minimum is DC.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite DC constraint system has a single-inequality normal form, and the represented set class is closed under finite intersections and finite unions.
assumptions_latex: All sets use a common convex ambient domain \(C\).
All constraint families and set families are finite.
All constraint functions are finite DC functions on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finitely DC-inequality-represented subsets of \(C\) are closed under finite intersections and unions.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Inequality Normal Form and Finite Set Closure
DC Set Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite inequality representation of a DC set relative to a convex ambient set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex. A set \(D\subseteq C\) is called a finitely represented DC set relative to \(C\) if there exist finite convex functions \(g_i,h_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\), for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), such that
\[
D=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x\in C:g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le0\}.
\]
The definition concerns the representation of the set; it does not assert that \(D\) itself is convex. Different families of DC inequalities may represent the same geometric set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finitely represented DC set is the intersection, inside a convex ambient set, of finitely many DC sublevel regions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D=\bigcap_i\{x\in C:g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le0\}\) is a DC-set representation relative to \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC sets and DC-inequality projections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the stated DC-set class and relates it to sets defined by a single difference-of-convex inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set $M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is a DC set if there exist convex functions $g,h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $M=\{x:g(x)\le 0,\ h(x)\ge 0\}$. Then $M=\{x:\max\{g(x),-h(x)\}\le 0\}$. Conversely, if $S=\{x:g(x)-h(x)\le 0\}$ with $g$ and $h$ convex, then $S$ is the projection onto $\mathbb{R}^n$ of the DC set $\{(x,t):g(x)-t\le 0,\ t-h(x)\le 0\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DC set is defined by a convex sublevel constraint together with a reverse convex constraint. It admits a single DC-inequality description, while any set defined by one DC inequality is the projection of a DC set in one additional dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M=\{x:g(x)\le0,\ h(x)\ge0\}=\{x:\max\{g(x),-h(x)\}\le0\},\qquad \{x:g(x)-h(x)\le0\}=\operatorname{proj}_x\{(x,t):g(x)-t\le0,\ t-h(x)\le0\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Representation of Closed Sets by DC Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provides point separation and a countable DC-inequality representation for every nonempty closed proper subset of Euclidean space using any prescribed strictly convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be strictly convex, and let \(S\subsetneq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and closed. Then: (i) for every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus S\), there exists an affine function \(l\) such that \[l(y)-h(y)>0,\qquad l(x)-h(x)\le 0\quad\forall x\in S;\] and (ii) there exists a sequence of affine functions \((l_i)_{i\ge 1}\) such that \[S=\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty}\{x\mid l_i(x)-h(x)\le 0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any strictly convex real-valued h and any nonempty closed proper subset S of R^n, every point outside S is separated from S by an inequality l − h ≤ 0 with l affine, and S is the intersection of countably many such inequality sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus S\;\exists l\text{ affine}:\ l(y)-h(y)>0\ \land\ \forall x\in S,\ l(x)-h(x)\le 0\right]\land\left[\exists(l_i)_{i\ge1}\text{ affine}:\ S=\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty}\{x\mid l_i(x)-h(x)\le0\}\right]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Sets and Lifted DC-Inequality Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the stated notion of a DC set, its single-inequality form, and the lifted representation of a general DC-inequality set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(M\subset\mathbb R^n\) is called a DC set if there are convex functions \(g,h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) such that \(M=\{x:g(x)\leq0,\ h(x)\geq0\}\). It then also has the DC-inequality description \(M=\{x:\max\{g(x),-h(x)\}\leq0\}\). Conversely, if \(S=\{x:g(x)-h(x)\leq0\}\), where \(g,h\) are convex, then \(S=\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbb R^n}(\widetilde M)\), where \(\widetilde M=\{(x,t):g(x)-t\leq0,\ t-h(x)\leq0\}\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\) is a DC set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DC set is described by a convex sublevel condition together with a convex-function superlevel condition. Such a set has a single DC-inequality description. Conversely, a set defined by one DC inequality is the projection of a DC set in one additional dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M=\{x:g(x)\leq0,\ h(x)\geq0\}=\{x:\max\{g(x),-h(x)\}\leq0\},\qquad \{x:g(x)-h(x)\leq0\}=\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbb R^n}(\widetilde M)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex, Reverse-Convex, and DC Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies scalar inequalities according to the convex, concave, or DC structure of their defining functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inequality \(f(x)\le 0\) is called convex when \(f\) is convex. It is called reverse convex (or complementary convex) when \(f\) is concave; equivalently, it can be expressed as \(h(x)\ge 0\) for a convex function \(h=-f\). If \(f\) is DC, then \(f(x)\le 0\) is a DC inequality. The opposite direction \(f(x)\ge 0\) is also a DC inequality because \(-f\) is DC.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality f(x) ≤ 0 is convex when f is convex and reverse convex when f is concave; the latter can equivalently be written h(x) ≥ 0 with convex h. If f is DC, inequalities in either direction are DC inequalities because negation preserves the DC property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ DC}\implies -f\text{ DC},\quad\text{so both }f(x)\le 0\text{ and }f(x)\ge 0\text{ are DC inequalities}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-Set and Sequential Detection Properties of the Separation Functional
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes membership in the closed set using the separation functional defined from a strictly convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed, let \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be strictly convex, and let \(d\geq0\) be determined by
\[
d^2(x)=\inf_{\substack{y\in S\\p\in\partial h(x)}}\bigl[h(y)-h(x)-\langle p,y-x\rangle\bigr].
\]
Then \(d(x)=0\) for every \(x\in S\), \(d(x)>0\) for every \(x\notin S\), and, whenever \(x^k\to x\) and \(d(x^k)\to0\), one has \(x\in S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The separation functional vanishes on S, is strictly positive outside S, and detects membership at limits of convergent sequences whose functional values approach zero.
assumptions_latex: S\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and closed}
h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\text{ is strictly convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\forall x\in S,\ d(x)=0\bigr)\land\bigl(\forall x\notin S,\ d(x)>0\bigr)\land\bigl(x^k\to x,\ d(x^k)\to0\Rightarrow x\in S\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Constraint–Feasible-Region Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence between finite DC inequality systems and feasible regions represented relative to a convex ambient domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(f_i=g_i-h_i\), where \(g_i,h_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\) are finite convex functions. The feasible region of the finite DC system \(f_i(x)\le0\) is
\[
F=C\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le0\}.
\]
Conversely, every subset of \(C\) supplied with such a finite DC-inequality representation is the feasible region of a canonical DC constraint system. This is a representation correspondence and imposes no convexity or connectedness on \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite DC inequality descriptions and feasible regions of canonical DC constraint systems are the same represented objects relative to a convex ambient domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is exactly the feasible region represented by the finite DC inequality family.
knowledge_statements.title: DC Constraint–Feasible-Region Correspondence
DC Feasible-Region Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between finite DC-set descriptions and feasible regions of canonical DC inequality systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(f_i=g_i-h_i\), where \(g_i,h_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex. The feasible region of the system \(f_i(x)\le0\), for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), is exactly
\[
F=C\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le0\}.
\]
Conversely, every finitely represented DC set relative to \(C\) is the feasible region of such a finite DC inequality system. Thus finite DC-set geometry and canonical DC feasibility descriptions coincide at the level of represented subsets of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite DC inequality systems generate precisely the finitely represented DC sets in a convex ambient domain.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i,h_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\) are finite convex functions for finitely many indices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a finitely represented DC set, and every such set arises as a DC feasible region.

knowledge_statements.title: DC Set-to-Program Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact continuous minimization encoding of feasibility for a finite DC inequality description on a compact convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(D=\{x\in C:g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), where all \(g_i,h_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\) are continuous and convex. Define
\[
\Phi(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m[g_i(x)-h_i(x)]_+,
\qquad [g_i-h_i]_+=\max\{g_i,h_i\}-h_i.
\]
Then \(\Phi\) is continuous, DC, and nonnegative on \(C\), and
\[
D\ne\varnothing\iff\min_{x\in C}\Phi(x)=0,
\qquad D=\{x\in C:\Phi(x)=0\}.
\]
Thus set membership and feasibility are encoded exactly by a DC penalty program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact convex domain, summed positive violations of continuous DC constraints form a continuous nonnegative DC objective whose zero minimizers are exactly the feasible points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\ne\varnothing\) exactly when \(\min_{x\in C}\Phi(x)=0\), and \(D=\{x\in C:\Phi(x)=0\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Noncompact Zero-Infimum Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the zero-optimum feasibility test when the violation objective need not attain its infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Compactness or another attainment hypothesis is essential for the implication \(\inf_C\Phi=0\Rightarrow D\ne\varnothing\). Let \(C=\mathbb{R}\), impose \(e^x\le0\), and set \(\Phi(x)=[e^x]_+=e^x\). Then
\[
D=\varnothing,
\qquad
\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\Phi(x)=0.
\]
For an arbitrary domain, the pointwise identity \(D=\{x:\Phi(x)=0\}\) remains valid even when the zero-infimum test fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without attainment, an infeasible DC system can have violation infimum zero; only the zero-level-set identity remains unconditional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D=\varnothing\) and \(\inf_{x\in C}\Phi(x)=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical DC Program Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional constrained minimization in an explicitly scoped convex-difference objective and inequality convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Relative to a convex domain \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), a canonical DC program has the form
\[
\inf_{x\in C}\{g_0(x)-h_0(x):g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\},
\]
where \(g_i,h_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\) are finite convex functions. Equivalently, the objective can be epigraphed as
\[
\inf_{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb{R}}t
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
 g_0(x)-h_0(x)-t\le0,
\quad g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le0.
\]
This convention concerns model representation and does not imply that the feasible region is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical DC program minimizes a convex difference over a convex domain subject to finitely many convex-difference inequalities; its objective also has an exact epigraph DC encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed formulations are equivalent canonical DC programs.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical DC Program Form
Canonical DC Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional constrained minimization in standard difference-of-convex form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A canonical DC program on a convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) has the form
\[
\inf_{x\in C}\{g_0(x)-h_0(x):g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\},
\]
where every \(g_i,h_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and finite, including the objective pair indexed by \(0\). The feasible set may be nonconvex because subtracting \(h_i\) need not preserve convex sublevel geometry. A feasible point attaining the infimum, when one exists, is a global solution if its objective value is no larger than that of every other feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical DC program minimizes one convex difference over a convex domain subject to finitely many convex-difference inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed optimization problem is in canonical DC form.

knowledge_statements.title: Noncanonical DC Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reductions of common equality, maximum, and disjunctive DC constraints to canonical inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let all functions below be DC on a common convex domain \(C\). A DC equality \(f(x)=0\) is equivalent to the pair \(f(x)\le0\) and \(-f(x)\le0\). A finite maximum constraint satisfies
\[
\max_{1\le k\le r}f_k(x)\le0\iff f_k(x)\le0\quad(k=1,\ldots,r).
\]
A finite disjunction satisfies
\[
\bigvee_{k=1}^r[f_k(x)\le0]
\iff \min_{1\le k\le r}f_k(x)\le0.
\]
Because negation and finite minima preserve the DC class, these noncanonical constraint forms have exact canonical DC inequality encodings without changing their feasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DC equalities, finite maximum constraints, and finite disjunctions admit exact reformulations using canonical DC inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed transformations preserve the feasible set and yield canonical DC inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Partly Convex Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blockwise convexity with respect to designated variables, including the biconvex two-block specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^q\) be convex. A function \(f:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex in the \(x\)-block if \(x\mapsto f(x,y)\) is convex on \(X\) for every fixed \(y\in Y\). A model is partly convex when its objective or designated constraint functions possess convexity in at least one specified variable block while the remaining blocks are fixed. If both \(x\mapsto f(x,y)\) and \(y\mapsto f(x,y)\) are convex for every fixed complementary block, then \(f\) is biconvex. Blockwise convexity does not by itself imply joint convexity on \(X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partly convex model is convex in designated variable blocks with all complementary blocks fixed; biconvexity requires this for both blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convexity of the indicated partial mappings defines partial or biconvex structure, not necessarily joint convexity.

children.title: Convex–Concave Models
children.top_down_role: Models organized around interacting convex and concave components.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex–Concave Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-block saddle models with convex minimizing sections and concave maximizing sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^q\) be convex. A function \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex–concave when \(x\mapsto L(x,y)\) is convex on \(X\) for every \(y\in Y\), and \(y\mapsto L(x,y)\) is concave on \(Y\) for every \(x\in X\). The associated saddle model is
\[
\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y).
\]
A pair \((x^*,y^*)\in X\times Y\) is a saddle point when
\[
L(x^*,y)\le L(x^*,y^*)\le L(x,y^*)
\]
for every \(x\in X\) and \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex–concave model is convex in its minimizing block and concave in its maximizing block; saddle points satisfy the two-sided saddle inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The partial convexity and concavity conditions define the displayed saddle model and saddle-point predicate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–Dual Gap Saddle Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact nonnegative gap test and epsilon residual for a candidate saddle pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \((x,y)\in X\times Y\), suppose the following quantities are finite and define
\[
G(x,y)=\sup_{v\in Y}L(x,v)-\inf_{u\in X}L(u,y).
\]
Then \(G(x,y)\ge0\), and
\[
G(x,y)=0
\iff
L(x,v)\le L(x,y)\le L(u,y)
\quad(\forall u\in X,\ \forall v\in Y).
\]
Thus zero gap is equivalent to the saddle-point condition, while \(G(x,y)\le\varepsilon\) bounds the sum of the two unilateral saddle residuals by \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The saddle gap is nonnegative, vanishes exactly at saddle points, and provides an epsilon saddle residual.
assumptions_latex: \(L(x,y)\) is finite at the candidate pair.
The displayed supremum and infimum are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(x,y)=0\iff(x,y)\) is a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Gap Saddle Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimax Equality Can Fail Without Compactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noncompact convex–concave example with a strict extended-valued minimax gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=Y=(0,\infty)\) and \(L(x,y)=yx^2-x\). Each map \(L(\cdot,y)\) is convex and each map \(L(x,\cdot)\) is affine and hence concave, but
\[
\inf_{x>0}\sup_{y>0}L(x,y)=+\infty,
\qquad
\sup_{y>0}\inf_{x>0}L(x,y)=0.
\]
Therefore sectional convex–concavity alone does not imply minimax equality, finite minimax value, or saddle-point existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On noncompact blocks, a finite convex–concave function can have a strict minimax gap and no saddle point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_X\sup_YL=+\infty>0=\sup_Y\inf_XL\).
knowledge_statements.title: Minimax Equality Can Fail Without Compactness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compact Continuous Convex–Concave Minimax Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional compact continuous minimax equality and saddle-point existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^q\) be nonempty compact convex sets. If \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous, convex in \(x\) for every fixed \(y\), and concave in \(y\) for every fixed \(x\), then
\[
\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}L(x,y)=\max_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}L(x,y).
\]
Both extrema are attained, and every minimax optimizer paired with every maximin optimizer is a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous convex–concave function on compact convex blocks has equal attained minimax and maximin values and a saddle point.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty compact convex subsets of finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}L(x,y)=\max_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}L(x,y)\), with saddle-point attainment.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact Continuous Convex–Concave Minimax Theorem

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Convexity Representation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blockwise convexity is strictly weaker than joint convexity, even for smooth bilinear functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(X=Y=[-1,1]\), define \(f(x,y)=xy\). For every fixed \(y\), the mapping \(x\mapsto xy\) is affine and hence convex; likewise, for every fixed \(x\), the mapping \(y\mapsto xy\) is affine and convex. Thus \(f\) is biconvex. However,
\[
\nabla^2 f(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}
\]
has eigenvalues \(-1\) and \(1\), so \(f\) is neither jointly convex nor jointly concave on \([-1,1]^2\). Therefore partial or separate convexity cannot be substituted for joint convexity in convex-model representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bilinear function is convex in each variable separately but neither convex nor concave jointly, marking the boundary of partial-convexity claims.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Separate convexity of \(f\) does not imply joint convexity or joint concavity on \(X\times Y\).

knowledge_statements.title: Exact DC Global Optimality Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact objective-difference criterion for a finite-dimensional constrained DC minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(g,h:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex. For \(f=g-h\) and \(\bar x\in C\), the following condition is necessary and sufficient for global optimality:
\[
\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C} f(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
g(x)-g(\bar x)\ge h(x)-h(\bar x)\quad\text{for every }x\in C.
\]
Equivalently, the convex increment of \(g\) from \(\bar x\) dominates the convex increment of \(h\) at every feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point globally minimizes a DC objective exactly when every feasible increment of its first convex component dominates the corresponding increment of its second component.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) and \(h\) are finite convex functions on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}(g(x)-h(x))\) exactly under the displayed increment inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Level-Surface Normal-Cone Characterization of a Global Maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The preceding hypotheses on h and C are not reproduced in the extract; the normal cone uses the source's convention permitting reference points outside C.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the preceding assumptions, let \(\bar x\in C\) satisfy
\[
-\infty\le \inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}h(x)<h(\bar x).
\]
Then \(\bar x\) is a global maximizer of \(h\) on \(C\) if and only if
\[
\partial h(x)\subseteq N(C,x)
\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n\text{ such that }h(x)=h(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assume x-bar lies in C and its h-value is strictly above the global infimum. Under the preceding hypotheses, x-bar globally maximizes h on C exactly when, at every ambient point on the same level surface, the subdifferential of h is contained in the extended normal cone of C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General convex-analysis definition. The source display inconsistently uses f instead of the introduced function \varphi; the notation is normalized here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \varphi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}, let \varphi(\bar x)<+\infty, and let \varepsilon\ge 0. The \varepsilon-subdifferential of \varphi at \bar x is
\[
\partial_\varepsilon\varphi(\bar x)=\left\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:\varphi(x)\ge \varphi(\bar x)+\langle s,x-\bar x\rangle-\varepsilon\ \text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R}^n\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epsilon-subdifferential consists of vectors giving a global affine lower support to the function up to additive error epsilon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_\varepsilon\varphi(\bar x)=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ \varphi(x)\ge\varphi(\bar x)+\langle s,x-\bar x\rangle-\varepsilon\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: All-Epsilon DC Inclusion Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact global DC optimality characterized by epsilon-subdifferential inclusion for finite convex components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g,h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be finite convex functions and \(\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). For \(\varepsilon\ge0\), let
\[
\partial_\varepsilon q(\bar x)=\{y:q(x)\ge q(\bar x)+\langle y,x-\bar x\rangle-\varepsilon\ \forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.
\]
Then
\[
\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}(g-h)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\partial_\varepsilon h(\bar x)\subseteq\partial_\varepsilon g(\bar x)\quad\forall\varepsilon\ge0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point globally minimizes a finite-valued DC function exactly when every epsilon-subgradient of the subtracted component is an epsilon-subgradient of the first component for every nonnegative epsilon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}(g-h)\) exactly under the all-epsilon inclusions.
knowledge_statements.title: All-Epsilon DC Inclusion Criterion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ordinary Common Subgradients Do Not Certify Global DC Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of replacing all-epsilon inclusion by ordinary common-subgradient stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(\mathbb{R}\), let \(g(x)=0\) and \(h(x)=x^2\). At \(\bar x=0\),
\[
\partial g(0)=\partial h(0)=\{0\},
\]
but \((g-h)(x)=-x^2\) is unbounded below. Thus a common ordinary subgradient does not imply global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common ordinary subgradient is only a criticality condition: for zero minus x-squared it holds at zero although the DC objective is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial g(0)\cap\partial h(0)\ne\varnothing\) does not imply \(0\in\operatorname*{argmin}(g-h)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary Common Subgradients Do Not Certify Global DC Optimality
DC Inclusion Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global optimality expressed through all approximate subdifferentials of the convex components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Extend \(g\) and \(h\) by \(+\infty\) outside the closed convex feasible set \(C\). For \(\varepsilon\ge0\), define
\[
\partial_\varepsilon q(\bar x)=\{y:q(x)\ge q(\bar x)+\langle y,x-\bar x\rangle-\varepsilon\ \text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.
\]
If \(g,h\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions and \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}g\cap\operatorname{dom}h\), then
\[
\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}(g-h)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\partial_\varepsilon h(\bar x)\subseteq\partial_\varepsilon g(\bar x)
\quad\text{for every }\varepsilon\ge0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is globally DC-optimal exactly when every epsilon-subgradient of the subtracted convex component is an epsilon-subgradient of the first component, for every epsilon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\) is globally optimal if and only if \(\partial_\varepsilon h(\bar x)\subseteq\partial_\varepsilon g(\bar x)\) for every \(\varepsilon\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Feasibility Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines inclusion checking through the feasibility of a set difference and records which set depends on the reference point in two associated formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For sets \(D\) and \(C\), checking whether \(D\subseteq C\), equivalently determining whether the inclusion
\[
x\in D\setminus C
\]
has a solution, is called the DC feasibility problem. Thus
\[
D\subseteq C\iff D\setminus C=\varnothing.
\]
For concave minimization, \(C=\{x\mid f(x)\geq f(x^0)\}\) depends on \(x^0\); for the canonical DC program, \(D=\{x\in G\mid l(x)\leq l(x^0)\}\) depends on \(x^0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The DC feasibility problem checks whether D is contained in C by determining whether D minus C contains a point. The inclusion holds exactly when that set difference is empty. In concave minimization, C depends on the reference point x⁰; in the canonical DC program, D depends on x⁰.
assumptions_latex: D,C\text{ are subsets of a common ambient space}.
x^0\text{ is the reference point in the stated concave-minimization or canonical-DC formulation}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\subseteq C\iff D\setminus C=\varnothing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Additive Approximate DC Inclusion Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive global near-optimality for finite convex DC components, characterized by shifted epsilon-subdifferential inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g,h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be finite convex functions, \(\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\delta\ge0\). Define \(\partial_\varepsilon q(\bar x)=\{y:q(x)\ge q(\bar x)+\langle y,x-\bar x\rangle-\varepsilon\ \forall x\}\). Then
\[
g(\bar x)-h(\bar x)\le \inf_x(g(x)-h(x))+\delta
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularity of Paired Level-Constrained Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines regularity through invariance of the optimal value under strict replacement of a level constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha,\gamma\in\overline{\mathbb R}\), a closed set \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and functions \(f,h:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), consider \(P_\alpha=\inf\{f(x):x\in\Omega,\ h(x)\geq\alpha\}\) and \(Q_\gamma=\sup\{h(x):x\in\Omega,\ f(x)\leq\gamma\}\). Problem \(P_\alpha\) is regular if \(\inf P_\alpha=\inf\{f(x):x\in\Omega,\ h(x)>\alpha\}\). Problem \(Q_\gamma\) is regular if \(\sup Q_\gamma=\sup\{h(x):x\in\Omega,\ f(x)<\gamma\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each paired problem is regular when replacing its non-strict level constraint by the corresponding strict constraint leaves its optimal value unchanged.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC* polar polyhedral set-inclusion procedure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterative polar outer-approximation procedure for either proving \(D\subset C\) or finding a point in \(D\setminus C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a polyhedron \(D\), a closed convex set \(C\), and a vertex \(x^0\in D\cap\operatorname{int}C\), translate \(D,C\) and the canonical cone at \(x^0\) by \(-x^0\). Choose edge points \(z^i\), taking the intersection with \(\partial C\) when it exists, and initialize \(P_1=\{y:\langle z^i,y\rangle\le1,\ i=1,\ldots,n\}\). At iteration \(k\), solve \(\mu(v)=\max\{\langle v,x\rangle:x\in D\}\) at the required vertices of \(P_k\), with basic optimizer \(x(v)\), and select \(v^k\in\arg\max_{v\in V_k}\mu(v)\). If \(\mu(v^k)\le1\), return the certificate \(C^\circ\subset D^\circ\), hence \(D\subset C\). If \(\mu(v^k)>1\) and \(x^k:=x(v^k)\notin C\), return \(x^k\in D\setminus C\). Otherwise choose \(\theta_k\ge1\) with \(\widehat x^k=\theta_kx^k\in\partial C\), set \(P_{k+1}=P_k\cap\{y:\theta_k\langle x^k,y\rangle\le1\}\), compute its vertices, and repeat using the newly created vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DC* builds and successively refines a polyhedral outer approximation of the polar of C. Linear programs over D either certify polar containment and thus D contained in C, produce a point of D outside C, or generate a boundary-based cut and continue.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is a closed convex set}
z^i\text{ is the intersection of the }i\text{-th canonical-cone edge with }\partial C\text{ when it exists, and otherwise any point on that edge}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure returns either }x\in D\setminus C\text{ or a certificate }C^\circ\subset D^\circ\Rightarrow D\subset C,\text{ unless another refinement is performed.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar-approximation algorithm for LRCP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral refinement in polar space, including the stated global-optimality and infeasibility termination certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume (51). Initialize an incumbent \(\bar x\), with \(\bar x=\varnothing\) if no feasible solution is known, and construct \(S_1\supset C^*\) with vertex set \(V_1\). At iteration \(k\), compute \(s(v)=\max\{\langle v,x\rangle:x\in\Omega,\;cx\le c\bar x\}\) for each \(v\in V_k\), and choose \(v^k\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in V_k}s(v)\). If \(s(v^k)\le1\), then \(C^*\subset[D(\bar x)]^*\), certifying that \(\bar x\) is globally optimal when \(\bar x\ne\varnothing\), or that (LRCP) is infeasible when \(\bar x=\varnothing\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm repeatedly solves a maximization problem at every vertex of a polyhedral outer approximation of the polar set. A maximum value at most one certifies global optimality of the incumbent, or infeasibility if no incumbent exists; otherwise a boundary point supplies a new polar cut and may update the incumbent.

\(\bar x\) is a feasible incumbent, or \(\bar x=\varnothing\) if none is known.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower-conjugate dual construction, attainment, and symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract relies on standing hypotheses for the primal problem, set X, and function f that are not restated in this item.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
X^{\natural}=\{p\in\mathbb R_+^n:p^Tx\le 1\ \forall x\in X\}=X^\circ\cap\mathbb R_+^n.
\]
Under the standing hypotheses, \(X^{\natural}\) is compact and convex with nonempty relative interior in \(\mathbb R_+^n\), and
\[
X=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:p^Tx\le1\ \forall p\in X^{\natural}\}.
\]
The lower-conjugate dual is
\[
(DP)\qquad \max\{f^{\natural}(p):p\in X^{\natural}\}.
\]
The function \(f^{\natural}\) is continuous, so \((DP)\) attains an optimum. If \((f^{\natural})^{\natural}=f\), then the dual of \((DP)\) is the primal problem. For primal and dual optimizers \(\bar x,\bar p\),
\[
1-f(\bar x)f^{\natural}(\bar p)\ge0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower conjugate of X is its nonnegative polar slice. Under the section's standing hypotheses it is compact and convex with nonempty interior, and conjugating it again recovers X. Maximizing the lower conjugate of f over this set defines the dual problem; continuity gives dual attainment, biconjugacy makes the duality symmetric, and one minus the product of primal and dual objective values is nonnegative.
assumptions_latex: \text{The standing hypotheses of the primal problem ensure the asserted compactness, interior, continuity, and biconjugacy properties.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simplicial cutting-plane partition algorithm for a DC problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm and its finite termination tests and asymptotic convergence condition for problem (Q).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the DC problem $(Q)$ have objective $G-H$ on a feasible set $M\subseteq S_0$, where $S_0$ is an $m$-simplex, $x^0\in M$, and supporting affine functions of $H$ can be formed from $p^k\in\partial H(x^k)$. Maintain the piecewise-affine model $L_{k+1}=\max\{L_k,l_k\}$, solve $LP(L_k,S)$ on the active simplices, update the incumbent $(\bar x,\gamma)$, and discard every simplex whose bound satisfies $\alpha(S)\leq\gamma$. Select a remaining simplex of maximal $\alpha(S)$ and refine it radially at $x^k$ unless its subdivision counter is a multiple of $N$ or $x^k$ is a vertex, in which case bisect its longest edge. If no simplex remains, $\bar x$ solves $(Q)$; if $L_k(x^k)=H(x^k)$ and $x^k$ is a vertex of the selected simplex, then $x^k$ solves $(Q)$. The periodic longest-edge bisection rule makes the subdivision process normal, yielding convergence under the applicable general partition-convergence assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from a simplex containing the feasible set and an incumbent feasible point. Repeatedly solve the model LP on active simplices, prune simplices whose bounds cannot improve the incumbent, strengthen the piecewise-affine support model of H, and subdivide the selected simplex either radially or by longest-edge bisection. Exhaustion of the active set or exact contact at a selected vertex certifies a global solution of (Q). Periodic longest-edge bisection ensures normal subdivision and hence convergence under the general partition-search assumptions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General convex-analysis definition used here as supporting notation for DC global-optimality theory.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual CS/OA algorithm for CDC
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cone-cover refinement and polar outer approximation for the quasiconcave dual problem; the extracted terminal status clause contains an unresolved inconsistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume (48) and \(0\in\operatorname{int}\Omega\). Initialize \(S_1\supset C^*\), a cone cover \(\mathcal S\) of \(S_1\), an active collection \(\mathcal R\), and an incumbent \(\bar y\) for (QCM), taking \(\gamma=\varphi(\bar y)\) or \(\gamma=+\infty\) when none is known.
