children.title: Concave-Minimization Branching Regimes
children.top_down_role: Partition choices used to organize concave-minimization search trees.

knowledge_statements.title: Concave-Minimization Branching Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive, best-bound, and depth-first node-selection regimes within spatial branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a finite live-node set \(\mathcal{L}_k\), where each node \(N\) represents a compact region \(R_N\) and has a valid lower bound \(L_N\). A branching regime selects either all eligible nodes, a best-bound node \(N_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{N\in\mathcal{L}_k}L_N\), or a deepest live node. It replaces each selected node by finitely many children whose regions cover \(R_N\), removes fathomed children, and retains all others. Ties are resolved by a fixed deterministic rule; the incumbent is updated whenever a feasible point with smaller objective value is found.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branching regime specifies which live regions are split next while preserving coverage, valid bounds, and the current best feasible solution.
assumptions_latex: Every live node has a valid regional lower bound.
Children of a branched node cover the parent region.
The node-selection and tie-breaking rules are deterministic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each regime preserves all nonfathomed regions and yields a well-defined deterministic search sequence.

notation.meaning: feasible region represented by node N
valid lower bound at node N

children.title: Concave-Minimization Node Bounds
children.top_down_role: Regional bounds associated with nodes in concave-minimization search.

knowledge_statements.title: Concave-Minimization Node Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regional lower and upper bounds used to certify branch-and-bound decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be the original feasible set, let \(f^*=\min_{x\in P}f(x)\), and let every live node \(N\in\mathcal{L}\) represent a region \(R_N\subseteq P\) with a bound \(L_N\leq f(x)\) for all \(x\in R_N\). Let \(\bar x\in P\) be an incumbent and set \(U=f(\bar x)\). If the live regions contain every point that has not been safely fathomed, define \(L=\min\bigl(\{U\}\cup\{L_N:N\in\mathcal{L}\}\bigr)\). Then \(L\leq f^*\leq U\), including when \(\mathcal{L}=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid live-node lower bounds, combined with the feasible incumbent value, bracket the global optimum even when the live set is empty.
assumptions_latex: Every point outside the live-node regions has been removed by a valid fathoming rule.
The incumbent \(\bar x\) is feasible for the original problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\leq f^*\leq U\), and \(U-L\leq\varepsilon\) implies \(f(\bar x)-f^*\leq\varepsilon\) for every \(\varepsilon\geq0\).

notation.meaning: lower bound associated with live node N
aggregate global lower bound including the incumbent value
objective value of the feasible incumbent
global minimum over the original feasible set

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relaxation Construction of a Valid Node Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic construction of a regional lower bound from an objective underestimator and an outer relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a node have feasible region \(R_N\), let \(Q_N\supseteq R_N\), and let \(\underline f_N:Q_N\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) satisfy \(\underline f_N(x)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in R_N\). Then \(L_N=\inf_{x\in Q_N}\underline f_N(x)\) satisfies \(L_N\leq\inf_{x\in R_N}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a valid objective underestimator over an outer relaxation produces a valid node lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_N\leq\inf_{x\in R_N}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: outer relaxation of the node region

children.title: Concave-Minimization Fathoming Criteria
children.top_down_role: Structural criteria for eliminating regions from further search.

knowledge_statements.title: Concave-Minimization Fathoming Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe node-deletion predicates for deterministic concave-minimization search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let node \(N\) represent \(R_N\), let \(L_N\leq\min_{x\in R_N}f(x)\), let \(U\) be the value of a feasible incumbent, and fix \(\varepsilon\geq0\). The node may be fathomed if \(R_N=\varnothing\), or if \(L_N\geq U-\varepsilon\). It may also be fathomed when a feasible point \(z_N\in R_N\) satisfies \(f(z_N)=L_N\), provided the incumbent is first updated to \(U\leftarrow\min\{U,f(z_N)\}\). For \(\varepsilon=0\), the bound test is \(L_N\geq U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discard an infeasible or sufficiently bounded node, or discard an exactly solved node after first incorporating its optimizer into the incumbent.
assumptions_latex: \(L_N\) is a valid lower bound on \(R_N\).
\(U\) is the objective value of a feasible incumbent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After any required incumbent update, a fathomed node contains no \(x\) satisfying \(f(x)<U-\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: feasible point attaining the node lower bound

children.title: Concave-Minimization Tree Growth
children.top_down_role: Tree-size behavior across alternative partition geometries.

knowledge_statements.title: Concave-Minimization Tree Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage and size invariants for finitely branching spatial search trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the root represent a feasible region \(P\) with objective \(f:P\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(U\) be a feasible incumbent value, fix \(\varepsilon\geq0\), and let \(b\geq1\) be an integer. Suppose each branching operation replaces one live node \(N\) by at most \(b\) children whose regions cover \(R_N\). After \(k\geq0\) branching operations, at most \(1+bk\) nodes have been generated and at most \(1+(b-1)k\) nodes are live before fathoming. If only nodes containing no point \(x\) with \(f(x)<U-\varepsilon\) are fathomed, every such potentially improving point remains in a live-node region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite branching gives linear generated-node and live-node bounds while valid fathoming preserves coverage of every point that could improve the incumbent beyond tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Each branching operation replaces one live node by at most \(b<\infty\) children.
Child regions cover their parent region.
Only nodes satisfying a valid fathoming criterion are deleted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathcal{T}_k|\leq1+bk\), \(|\mathcal{L}_k|\leq1+(b-1)k\), and every \(x\in P\) satisfying \(f(x)<U-\varepsilon\) remains covered by a live node.

notation.meaning: set of nodes generated after k branching operations
set of live nodes after k branching operations
maximum number of children per branch

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exponential Tree Growth with Depth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case size of a bounded-arity concave-minimization search tree when fathoming is ineffective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every nonleaf node has at most \(b\geq2\) children and the tree has depth at most \(d\), then it has at most \(b^d\) leaves and at most \(\sum_{i=0}^{d}b^i=(b^{d+1}-1)/(b-1)\) total nodes. Both bounds are attained by the complete \(b\)-ary tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded branching arity still permits exponentially many leaves and nodes as a function of depth.
assumptions_latex: Every node has at most \(b\) children.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\mathcal L|\leq b^d,\qquad |\mathcal T|\leq\frac{b^{d+1}-1}{b-1},\text{ and both bounds are sharp.}

children.title: Fixed-Charge Models
children.top_down_role: Concave-model reductions arising from fixed activation costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Charge Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concave-cost representation of nonnegative activities carrying activation charges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(x_i\in[0,u_i]\), \(u_i>0\), \(F_i\geq0\), and \(c_i\geq0\), and define \(\phi_i(0)=0\) and \(\phi_i(x_i)=F_i+c_i x_i\) for \(x_i>0\). Each \(\phi_i\) is concave on \([0,u_i]\), possibly with an upward jump to its right at zero. The fixed-charge problem is \(\min\{\sum_{i=1}^m\phi_i(x_i):x\in X\}\), where \(X\subseteq\prod_{i=1}^m[0,u_i]\). An activated formulation introduces \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\), imposes \(0\leq x_i\leq u_i y_i\), and minimizes \(\sum_{i=1}^m(F_i y_i+c_i x_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed charge can be represented as a concave activity cost or through a binary activation variable and an upper-linking constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\prod_{i=1}^m[0,u_i]\) contains the remaining constraints and does not impose additional conditions on the activation variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every feasible activity vector \(x\), minimizing the activated objective over linked binary vectors \(y\) gives \(\sum_{i=1}^m\phi_i(x_i)\); hence the two optimization formulations have the same optimal value and optimal activity vectors.

notation.meaning: fixed activation charge for activity i

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Fixed Charge Problems p. 62

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Linking Bound Requirement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for the standard binary activation formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The constraint \(0\leq x\leq uy\), \(y\in\{0,1\}\), represents \(x=0\) when inactive and \(0\leq x\leq u\) when active only when \(u\) is a valid finite upper bound. An underestimated bound removes intended active values; without a finite valid bound, this standard finite big-\(M\) representation is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The usual binary-linking formulation requires a valid finite activity bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq x\leq uy\) exactly represents the intended bounded activation domain when \(u\) is a valid finite upper bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Linking Bound Requirement

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Envelope of a Capacitated Fixed Charge
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact one-dimensional convexification of a fixed-charge cost with finite capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi(0)=0\) and \(\phi(x)=F+cx\) for \(0<x\leq u\), where \(F,c\geq0\) and \(u>0\). Then \[\operatorname{vex}_{[0,u]}\phi(x)=\left(c+\frac Fu\right)x.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex envelope of a capacitated fixed-charge cost is the chord joining zero and capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{vex}_{[0,u]}\phi(x)=(c+F/u)x\).

notation.meaning: convex envelope of the fixed-charge function

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Envelope of a Capacitated Fixed Charge

children.title: Economies-of-Scale Models
children.top_down_role: Concave-model reductions arising from decreasing marginal costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Economies-of-Scale Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous activity costs whose marginal or average cost decreases with scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^m\) and let \(u_i>0\). An economies-of-scale minimization model has the form \(\min\{\sum_{i=1}^m\phi_i(x_i):x\in X,\ 0\leq x_i\leq u_i\}\), where each \(\phi_i:[0,u_i]\to\mathbb{R}\) is nondecreasing and concave. If \(\phi_i(0)=0\), concavity implies that the average cost \(\phi_i(t)/t\) is nonincreasing for \(t>0\). When differentiable, concavity equivalently makes the marginal cost \(\phi_i'(t)\) nonincreasing. Minimizing these concave costs over a convex feasible region is generally a nonconvex optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Economies of scale are modeled by nondecreasing concave activity costs, yielding decreasing average cost and, when differentiable, decreasing marginal cost.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\phi_i\) is finite, nondecreasing, and concave on \([0,u_i]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\phi_i(0)=0\), then \(0<s<t\leq u_i\) implies \(\phi_i(s)/s\geq\phi_i(t)/t\).

source_refs.locator: Concave Minimization: Theory, Applications and Algorithms p. 43; 4. Basic Properties of Concave Minimization Problems p. 58

source_witnesses.locator: Concave Minimization: Theory, Applications and Algorithms p. 43; 4. Basic Properties of Concave Minimization Problems p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subadditivity of Concave Scale Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregation property of normalized concave activity costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi:[0,u]\to\mathbb R\) be concave with \(\phi(0)=0\). For all \(s,t\geq0\) satisfying \(s+t\leq u\), \[\phi(s+t)\leq\phi(s)+\phi(t).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave scale cost normalized to zero is subadditive on its capacity interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi(s+t)\leq\phi(s)+\phi(t)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Subadditivity of Concave Scale Costs

children.title: Fixed-Charge Scale-Economy Hybrids
children.top_down_role: Models combining activation costs with scale-dependent production structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Charge Scale-Economy Hybrids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hybrid separable costs combining activation charges with continuous concave operating costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(x_i\in[0,u_i]\), \(F_i\geq0\), and let \(g_i:[0,u_i]\to\mathbb{R}_+\) be nondecreasing and concave with \(g_i(0)=0\). Define \(\phi_i(0)=0\) and \(\phi_i(x_i)=F_i+g_i(x_i)\) for \(x_i>0\). Then \(\phi_i\) is concave on \([0,u_i]\), and the hybrid problem is \(\min\{\sum_{i=1}^m\phi_i(x_i):x\in X\}\). An activated formulation introduces \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\), imposes \(0\leq x_i\leq u_i y_i\), and minimizes \(\sum_{i=1}^m(F_i y_i+g_i(x_i))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hybrid model combines an activation charge with a concave operating cost and has an equivalent binary-linked value formulation.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_i\) is nonnegative, nondecreasing, concave, and satisfies \(g_i(0)=0\).
\(X\subseteq\prod_{i=1}^m[0,u_i]\) contains the remaining constraints and imposes no additional conditions on the activation variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every feasible activity vector \(x\), minimizing the activated objective over linked binary vectors \(y\) gives \(\sum_{i=1}^m\phi_i(x_i)\); consequently the two formulations have the same optimal value and optimal activity vectors.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Envelope of a Capacitated Hybrid Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scalar convexification of a fixed charge plus concave operating cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi(0)=0\) and \(\phi(x)=F+g(x)\) for \(0<x\leq u\), where \(F\geq0\), \(u>0\), and \(g:[0,u]\to\mathbb R_+\) is finite and concave with \(g(0)=0\). Then \[\operatorname{vex}_{[0,u]}\phi(x)=\frac{F+g(u)}{u}x.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex envelope of a capacitated fixed-charge scale-economy cost is its endpoint chord.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is finite, nonnegative, and concave on \([0,u]\), with \(g(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{vex}_{[0,u]}\phi(x)=x(F+g(u))/u\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Envelope of a Capacitated Hybrid Cost

children.title: Multiplicative Model Reductions
children.top_down_role: Direct concave reductions for multiplicative model structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicative Model Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive finite products reduced by a monotone logarithmic transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m f_i(x)\) and \(L(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\log f_i(x)\). Positivity makes both objectives finite, and \(L(x)=\log F(x)\). Hence \(F(x)\leq F(y)\) if and only if \(L(x)\leq L(y)\) for all \(x,y\in C\). Moreover, each \(\log f_i\) is concave, so \(L\) is concave. Thus minimizing the multiplicative model over \(C\) is exactly reducible to concave minimization of \(L\), with identical global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive product of concave factors on a convex feasible set has the same minimizers as the concave sum of their logarithms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\prod_{i=1}^m f_i(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\sum_{i=1}^m\log f_i(x)\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict-Positivity Boundary of Log Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain boundary for an exact finite real logarithmic formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite real-valued identity \(\log\prod_i f_i=\sum_i\log f_i\) requires \(f_i(x)>0\) for every included factor and feasible \(x\). If a factor can vanish, the logarithmic objective takes the extended value \(-\infty\); if a factor can be negative, the real logarithmic formulation is undefined and need not preserve product ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict positivity is essential for the stated finite log-sum reduction; zeros require extended values, and negative factors invalidate it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated finite real logarithmic reduction requires every included factor to be strictly positive throughout the feasible domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Multiplicative Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive weighted-product variant of logarithmic reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_i\geq0\), not all zero, and let \(f_i:C\to(0,\infty)\). Then \[F_a(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m f_i(x)^{a_i},\qquad L_a(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m a_i\log f_i(x)=\log F_a(x)\] have identical orderings and global minimizers. If \(C\) is convex and every \(f_i\) with \(a_i>0\) is concave, then \(L_a\) is concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive weighted product reduces exactly to a weighted sum of logarithms, which is concave for nonnegative weights and positive concave factors.
assumptions_latex: For the curvature conclusion, \(C\) is convex and each positively weighted factor is concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_C F_a=\operatorname*{argmin}_C L_a\), and \(L_a\) is concave under the curvature assumptions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adaptive interval-underestimation algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional adaptive partition algorithm for minimizing g on the bounded interval determined by the multiplicative reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\epsilon\geq0\), compute \(\underline\zeta,\bar\zeta\), initialize the partition with \([\underline\zeta,\bar\zeta]\), set \(U_0(\zeta)=U(\zeta;\underline\zeta,\bar\zeta)\), and let \(k=0\). At iteration \(k\), choose \[\zeta_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\zeta\in[\underline\zeta,\bar\zeta]}U_k(\zeta).\] If \(g(\zeta_k)-U_k(\zeta_k)\leq\epsilon\), return \(\zeta^\epsilon=\zeta_k\). Otherwise, split the current partition interval \([\zeta_s,\zeta_t]\ni\zeta_k\) at \(\zeta_k\), replace its underestimator pieces by \(U(\zeta;\zeta_s,\zeta_k)\) and \(U(\zeta;\zeta_k,\zeta_t)\), retain \(U_k\) elsewhere, increment \(k\), and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize a single interval and its endpoint-based underestimator. Repeatedly minimize the current piecewise underestimator. Stop when the true-value minus lower-bound gap at the selected point is at most epsilon; otherwise split the containing interval at that point, update its two underestimator pieces, and continue.
assumptions_latex: \(\underline\zeta\text{ and }\bar\zeta\text{ are computed as prescribed by the reformulation.}\)
\(U(\cdot;\zeta_s,\zeta_t)\text{ is the prescribed interval underestimator of }g.\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(\zeta^\epsilon)-U_k(\zeta^\epsilon)\leq\epsilon\text{ upon termination.}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interpolation, regularity, and intersection properties of the auxiliary function family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the source's three properties of the family \(\mathcal G\) on the positive zeta-domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \((\zeta_s,g_s),(\zeta_t,g_t)\in\mathbb R^2\) with \(0<\zeta_s<\zeta_t\), there is a unique member of \(\mathcal G\) determined by these points, namely \[\frac{g_s\zeta_s-g_t\zeta_t}{\zeta_s^2-\zeta_t^2}\,\zeta+\frac{g_s/\zeta_s-g_t/\zeta_t}{1/\zeta_s^2-1/\zeta_t^2}\,\frac1\zeta.\] Every member of \(\mathcal G\) is Lipschitz continuous on \(\{\zeta:\zeta\geq\zeta'\}\) for every \(\zeta'>0\). Any two distinct members of \(\mathcal G\) have at most one common point on \(\zeta>0\), and their derivatives differ at such a point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two values at distinct positive coordinates uniquely determine a member of G by the displayed linear-plus-reciprocal formula. Each member is Lipschitz on every positive half-line bounded away from zero. Two distinct members intersect at most once on the positive domain, with unequal derivatives at an intersection.
assumptions_latex: \((\zeta_s,g_s),(\zeta_t,g_t)\in\mathbb R^2\text{ and }0<\zeta_s<\zeta_t\) for the interpolation assertion.
\(g_1,g_2\in\mathcal G\text{ and }g_1\ne g_2\) for the intersection assertion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal G\text{ has unique two-point interpolation, every member is Lipschitz on each }[\zeta',\infty),\text{ and distinct members have at most one positive-domain intersection with unequal derivatives.}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concave reduction of multiplicative problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines multiplicative problems and records both the zero-factor boundary case and the positive concave-factor reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\ge 2\), \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and \(f(x)=\prod_{j=1}^p f_j(x)\), where \(f_j(x)\ge0\) on \(D\). If \(f_j(x^\circ)=0\) for some \(j\) and \(x^\circ\in D\), then the global minimum is \(0\) and \(x^\circ\) is globally optimal. Otherwise, if every \(f_j>0\) on \(D\) and every \(f_j:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is concave, then \[w_1(x)=\log f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^p\log f_j(x),\qquad w_2(x)=f(x)^{1/p}\] are concave on \(D\), and minimizing \(f\), \(w_1\), or \(w_2\) over \(D\) is equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiplicative problem minimizes a product of at least two nonnegative factors. A feasible zero factor yields the global value zero. If all factors are positive on the feasible set and concave, the logarithm and the pth root of the product are concave, strictly increasing transformations that preserve its global minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the concave reduction: }f_j(x)>0\text{ on }D\text{ and each }f_j:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\text{ is concave}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\exists x^\circ\in D,\exists j:f_j(x^\circ)=0\bigr)\Rightarrow \min_{x\in D}f(x)=0;\quad\text{otherwise }w_1,w_2\text{ are concave on }D\text{ and }\operatorname*{argmin}_D f=\operatorname*{argmin}_D w_1=\operatorname*{argmin}_D w_2.

knowledge_statements.title: Min–Max Model Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite convex min–max models represented by a scalar epigraph variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(E=\{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb{R}:f_i(x)\leq t\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m\}\). For every fixed \(x\in C\), the smallest feasible value of \(t\) is \(\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)\). Consequently, \(x^\star\) minimizes \(\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)\) over \(C\) if and only if \((x^\star,t^\star)\) minimizes \(t\) over \(E\), where \(t^\star=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x^\star)\). The set \(E\) is convex, and the lifted objective \(t\) is affine, hence both convex and concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite continuous convex min–max problem is exactly represented by minimizing an epigraph variable subject to all component bounds.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous and convex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in C}\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)=\min\{t:(x,t)\in E\}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simplex Representation of a Finite Maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise simplex representation underlying a finite min–max objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(z=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)\in\mathbb R^m\), \[\max_{1\leq i\leq m}z_i=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_m}\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i z_i,\qquad \Delta_m=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m:\sum_i\lambda_i=1\}.\] Consequently, \(\min_{x\in C}\max_i f_i(x)=\min_{x\in C}\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_m}\sum_i\lambda_i f_i(x)\), without implying interchange of the two optimization operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite maximum equals maximization of a convex combination over the probability simplex, but this identity alone does not permit swapping min and max.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_i z_i=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_m}\lambda^Tz\).
knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Representation of a Finite Maximum

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularity and max-residual formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded conditions for a continuous optimization problem over a set S.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The problem is regular when \(\min_{x\in S}f(x)=\inf_{x\in\operatorname{int}S}f(x)\). If \(f\) is continuous and \(S=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{int}S)\), then this regularity condition holds. For \(\alpha\in(-\infty,+\infty]\), define \(F(\alpha,x)=\sup\{f(x)-\alpha,g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regularity means that the minimum over S equals the infimum over the interior of S. Continuity of f and robustness of S, meaning that S is the closure of its interior, suffice for regularity. The associated max-residual function is the supremum of the objective-level residual and all constraint residuals.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the sufficient condition, }f\text{ is continuous and }S=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{int}S)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in S}f(x)=\inf_{x\in\operatorname{int}S}f(x),\qquad F(\alpha,x)=\sup\{f(x)-\alpha,g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x)\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relief Indicator Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded exact algorithm assuming each unconstrained relief-indicator subproblem is solved globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\alpha_1\in f(S)\) when a feasible solution is known, and otherwise set \(\alpha_1=+\infty\). For \(k=1,2,\ldots\), globally solve \[\mu_k=\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\varphi(\alpha_k,x)\] and let \(x^k\) be an optimizer. If \(\mu_k=0\), terminate with \(x^k\) globally optimal for \(\mathrm{(COP)}\); if \(\mu_k>0\), terminate with \(\mathrm{(COP)}\) infeasible. If \(\mu_k<0\), then \(x^k\in S\), \(f(x^k)<\alpha_k\), and the next level is \(\alpha_{k+1}=f(x^k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize the level from a known feasible objective value, or at positive infinity. At every iteration globally minimize the relief indicator. A zero minimum returns a global optimizer, a positive minimum certifies infeasibility, and a negative minimum supplies a strictly improving feasible point whose objective value becomes the next level.
assumptions_latex: \alpha_1\in f(S)\text{ if a feasible point is known; otherwise }\alpha_1=+\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu_k=0\Rightarrow x^k\text{ is globally optimal};\quad \mu_k>0\Rightarrow S=\varnothing;\quad \mu_k<0\Rightarrow x^k\in S,\ f(x^k)<\alpha_k,\ \alpha_{k+1}=f(x^k)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal-value characterization by a max-residual minimum

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\min_{x\in S}f(x)=\inf_{x\in\operatorname{int}S}f(x)\) and \(F(\alpha,x)=\sup\{f(x)-\alpha,g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x)\}\), then \[\alpha=\min_{x\in S}f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0=\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}F(\alpha,x).\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relief-separator conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition of level sets and the assumed separator family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha\in(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \[\widetilde S_\alpha=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:F(\alpha,x)\le0\}=\{x\in S:f(x)\le\alpha\}.\] Assume there is a function \(r(\alpha,x)\), lower semicontinuous in \(x\), such that (i) \(r(\alpha,x)=0\) for every \(x\in\widetilde S_\alpha\); (ii) \(0<r(\alpha,y)\le d(y,\widetilde S_\alpha):=\min_{x\in\widetilde S_\alpha}\|x-y\|\) for every \(y\notin\widetilde S_\alpha\); and (iii) for fixed \(x\), \(\alpha_1<\alpha_2\) implies \(r(\alpha_1,x)\ge r(\alpha_2,x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The alpha-sublevel feasible set is the zero sublevel set of F. A relief separator is assumed to be lower semicontinuous in x, zero on that set, strictly positive but no larger than the distance to it outside the set, and nonincreasing as the level alpha increases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r(\alpha,x)=0\ (x\in\widetilde S_\alpha),\quad 0<r(\alpha,y)\le d(y,\widetilde S_\alpha)\ (y\notin\widetilde S_\alpha),\quad \alpha_1<\alpha_2\Rightarrow r(\alpha_1,x)\ge r(\alpha_2,x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relief-indicator optimality and improvement certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded certificate for the continuous optimization problem (COP).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(S\ne\varnothing\) and define \(\varphi(\alpha,x)=h(\alpha,x)-\|x\|^2\). If \[\varphi(\alpha,\bar x)=0=\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\varphi(\alpha,x),\] then \(\bar x\) is a globally optimal solution of \(\mathrm{(COP)}\). Otherwise, \(\min_x\varphi(\alpha,x)<0\), and every \(x\) satisfying \(\varphi(\alpha,x)<0\) also satisfies \(x\in S\) and \(f(x)<\alpha\).

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicative Min–Max Hybrids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite products of positive pointwise maxima expanded into a min–max family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in C\), define \(H(x)=\prod_{j=1}^p\max_{i\in I_j}f_{ji}(x)\) and \(\mathcal A=\prod_{j=1}^p I_j\). Because all factors are positive and each index set is finite and nonempty, selections can be made independently in each factor. Therefore \(H(x)=\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A}\prod_{j=1}^p f_{j,\alpha_j}(x)\). The original multiplicative problem is consequently equivalent to a finite min–max problem indexed by \(\mathcal A\). Their optimal values coincide, and they have the same global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A product of positive finite maxima equals the maximum over all products obtained by selecting one term from each factor.
assumptions_latex: Every \(f_{ji}:C\to(0,\infty)\), with \(j=1,\ldots,p\) and \(i\in I_j\), is continuous.
Each index set \(I_j\) is finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in C}\prod_{j=1}^p\max_{i\in I_j}f_{ji}(x)=\min_{x\in C}\max_{\alpha\in\prod_{j=1}^p I_j}\prod_{j=1}^p f_{j,\alpha_j}(x)\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Explicit Expansion Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial size of the selection family produced by hybrid expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite nonempty index sets \(I_1,\ldots,I_p\), the selection set \(\mathcal A=\prod_{j=1}^p I_j\) has cardinality \[|\mathcal A|=\prod_{j=1}^p|I_j|.\] Thus explicit enumeration can be exponential in \(p\), even when the product-of-maxima expression is compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expanding a product of finite maxima creates the product of the component family sizes and can be exponentially larger than the compact expression.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathcal A|=\prod_j|I_j|\).
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Expansion Size

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Signed-Factor Failure of Independent Maximum Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for distributing products over independent maxima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Nonnegativity of all candidate factors is sufficient for \[\prod_{j=1}^p\max_{i\in I_j}a_{ji}=\max_{\alpha\in\prod_jI_j}\prod_{j=1}^pa_{j,\alpha_j}.\] Without this sign condition the identity can fail: if each of two factors has candidates \(\{-2,-1\}\), the product of the two maxima is \(1\), whereas the maximum selectable product is \(4\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent maximum selection distributes through products of nonnegative factors but can fail for signed factors.
assumptions_latex: The index sets are finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Signed factors do not in general satisfy the product-of-maxima expansion.
knowledge_statements.title: Signed-Factor Failure of Independent Maximum Selection

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar Parametric Reduction by a Second Linear Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal-value reduction to basic solutions of equality-sliced linear programs; no additional assumptions on F are stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\underline\alpha=\min\{\langle c^2,x\rangle:x\in D\}\) and \(\bar\alpha=\max\{\langle c^2,x\rangle:x\in D\}\). For every \(\alpha\in[\underline\alpha,\bar\alpha]\), let \(x^\alpha\) be a basic optimal solution of \(\min\{\langle c^1,x\rangle:x\in D,\ \langle c^2,x\rangle=\alpha\}\). Then \[\min_{x\in D}F(\langle c^1,x\rangle,\langle c^2,x\rangle)=\min_{\underline\alpha\leq\alpha\leq\bar\alpha}F(\langle c^1,x^\alpha\rangle,\langle c^2,x^\alpha\rangle).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If each level of the second linear form is represented by a basic solution minimizing the first linear form on that level, then optimizing F of the two linear forms over D reduces to optimizing F evaluated at those representatives over the scalar level interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in D}F(\langle c^1,x\rangle,\langle c^2,x\rangle)=\min_{\alpha\in[\underline\alpha,\bar\alpha]}F(\langle c^1,x^\alpha\rangle,\langle c^2,x^\alpha\rangle).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform approximation by DC functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform-density result on compact convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(E\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is compact and convex and \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) is continuous, then there exists a sequence \((g_k)_{k\ge1}\) of DC functions on \(E\) such that \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\sup_{x\in E}|g_k(x)-f(x)|=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every real-valued continuous function on a compact convex subset of Euclidean space is the uniform limit of a sequence of difference-of-convex functions on that set.
assumptions_latex: E\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is compact and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists (g_k)_{k\ge1}\text{ DC on }E\text{ such that }\|g_k-f\|_{\infty,E}\to0.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact continuous representation of binary restrictions by one concave inequality.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Deterministic Global Optimization: Approaches and Classes of Problems p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\phi(y)=\sum_{j=1}^q y_j(1-y_j)\) on \([0,1]^q\). Every summand is nonnegative on this box and vanishes exactly when \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\). Hence \(y\) is binary if and only if \(\phi(y)=0\), equivalently \(\phi(y)\leq0\). Since \(\phi\) is concave, binary restrictions in a mixed-integer model can be replaced exactly by box constraints and one reverse-convex inequality. The resulting continuous formulation preserves precisely the feasible points and objective values of the original model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary restrictions equal box constraints plus one concave inequality forcing the sum of fractionalness terms to vanish.
knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Programming Reductions

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 Deterministic Global Optimization: Approaches and Classes of Problems p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unit-Box Requirement for the Fractionalness Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the concave integrality inequality when its box restrictions are omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the scalar value \(y=2\), one has \(y(1-y)=-2\le0\), yet \(y\notin\{0,1\}\). Hence \(y(1-y)\le0\) enforces binarity only when combined with \(0\le y\le1\); the same failure applies componentwise to the aggregate inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without the unit-box constraints, the fractionalness inequality admits nonbinary values such as two.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y(1-y)\le0\not\Rightarrow y\in\{0,1\}
knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Box Requirement for the Fractionalness Inequality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded-Integer Binary Expansion Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact extension of the binary reduction route to finitely bounded integer variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\in\mathbb Z\) satisfy \(\ell\le z\le u\), where \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z\), and set \(m=\lceil\log_2(u-\ell+1)\rceil\). The restriction is represented exactly by \(z=\ell+\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}2^ky_k\), \(z\le u\), and \(y_k\in\{0,1\}\). Replacing the binary restrictions by \(0\le y\le1\) and \(\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}y_k(1-y_k)\le0\) gives an exact continuous reverse-convex formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finitely bounded integer variable can be binary encoded and represented exactly by box constraints and one concave integrality inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(z\) is required to be integer with \(\ell\le z\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z\in\mathbb Z\cap[\ell,u]\iff\exists y\in[0,1]^m:\ z=\ell+\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}2^ky_k,\ z\le u,\ \sum_{k=0}^{m-1}y_k(1-y_k)\le0
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Integer Binary Expansion Reduction

knowledge_statements.statement_title: McCormick Residual Bound on a Rectangle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative local consistency bound for bounded bilinear spatial refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\), \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\), and let \((x,y,w)\) satisfy the four McCormick inequalities for \(w=xy\) on this rectangle. Then \[|w-xy|\leq\frac{(u_x-\ell_x)(u_y-\ell_y)}4.\] Consequently, the maximum residual tends to zero along rectangles whose width product tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point in a McCormick relaxation has bilinear residual at most one quarter of the product of the interval widths.
assumptions_latex: \((x,y,w)\) satisfies all four McCormick inequalities on that rectangle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|w-xy|\leq (u_x-\ell_x)(u_y-\ell_y)/4\).
knowledge_statements.title: McCormick Residual Bound on a Rectangle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spatial Branch-and-Bound for Bounded Bilinear Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: McCormick spatial-search route for a bounded model whose exposed nonconvexities are lifted bilinear equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a compact model with lifted relations \(w_q=x_{i_q}x_{j_q}\), with the remaining node formulation convex. A node \(B\) is a product box for the participating variables. Its relaxation replaces every product graph by its four McCormick inequalities on \(B\). Maintain live boxes, a verified feasible incumbent \(U\), and valid lower bounds \(L(B)\). Select a live box; fathom it if its relaxation is infeasible or \(L(B)\ge U-\varepsilon\). Otherwise update \(U\) using any verified feasible point and bisect a factor interval of a product having nonzero relaxation residual, installing two covering children with recomputed envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch on bounded product factors, solve McCormick node relaxations, update only with genuinely feasible points, and prune only by infeasibility or certified bounds.
assumptions_latex: All factors in lifted bilinear terms have finite node bounds.
The non-product part of every node relaxation is convex and valid.
Every child pair covers its parent box.
Every node lower bound is valid for the original restricted model.
Every incumbent is feasible for the original bilinear model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No fathoming step removes a feasible point with objective value less than \(U-\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Current box for variables participating in bilinear products.
Valid lower bound for node B.

knowledge_statements.title: Spatial Branch-and-Bound for Bounded Bilinear Lifts

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bilinear Spatial Termination Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined global-bound and local product-consistency certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a verified feasible incumbent and \(\underline L=\min_{B\in\mathcal L}L(B)\), with \(\underline L=U\) if no live node remains. If the live boxes cover all unfathomed feasible points and \(U-\underline L\le\varepsilon\), then the incumbent is \(\varepsilon\)-global. On a live rectangle for product \(w_q=x_{i_q}x_{j_q}\), widths \(\Delta_{i_q},\Delta_{j_q}\) additionally certify \(|w_q-x_{i_q}x_{j_q}|\le\Delta_{i_q}\Delta_{j_q}/4\) throughout its McCormick relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible incumbent and minimum live-node bound certify global tolerance; rectangle widths separately certify bilinear residual tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is attained by a point feasible for the original model.
Live nodes cover all feasible points not already safely fathomed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U-f^*\le\varepsilon,\qquad |w_q-x_{i_q}x_{j_q}|\le\Delta_{i_q}\Delta_{j_q}/4\text{ on each live node}.

notation.meaning: Minimum valid lower bound over live nodes.
Current factor-interval widths for product q.

knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear Spatial Termination Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-Term Residual Depth Under Factor Bisection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local branch-depth bound for one bilinear product, not a global search-tree bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the initial rectangle for \(w=xy\) have widths \(\Delta_x,\Delta_y\). If every descendant step bisects one factor interval, then after \(t\) such steps on a branch the width product is \(\Delta_x\Delta_y2^{-t}\), and every McCormick-feasible point satisfies \(|w-xy|\le\Delta_x\Delta_y/(4\,2^t)\). Hence tolerance \(\eta>0\) is guaranteed once \(t\ge\max\{0,\lceil\log_2(\Delta_x\Delta_y/(4\eta))\rceil\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each factor bisection halves the scalar McCormick residual bound, giving logarithmic branch depth for a prescribed product tolerance.
assumptions_latex: One lifted product is refined at every counted descendant step.
Each counted step bisects exactly one factor interval.
McCormick inequalities are recomputed on every child.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: t\ge\max\left\{0,\left\lceil\log_2\frac{\Delta_x\Delta_y}{4\eta}\right\rceil\right\}\Longrightarrow |w-xy|\le\eta.

notation.meaning: Number of counted factor bisections along the branch.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Convergence of Fair Bilinear Spatial Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract convergence theorem for the specified bounded spatial route.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Apply the spatial scheme to a feasible compact model with continuous data and finite optimum. Assume live boxes always cover the unfathomed feasible set; every live box capable of attaining the smallest persistent lower bound is selected fairly; every infinite selected branch shrinks all participating factor intervals to zero; and node lower bounds are consistent, meaning that along a nested branch converging to \(x\), \(\liminf_kL(B_k)\ge f(x)\) whenever \(x\) is feasible. Assume also that refinement along boxes containing a global minimizer produces verified feasible incumbents whose values approach that minimizer's value. Then \(U_k-\underline L_k\to0\), where \(\underline L_k\) is the minimum live-node bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fair shrinking refinement, locally consistent bounds, and asymptotically complete feasible recovery make the certified global gap vanish.
assumptions_latex: The original feasible set is nonempty and compact and has finite optimum.
Live boxes cover every unfathomed feasible point.
Promising boxes are selected fairly and every infinite selected branch localizes.
Node lower bounds are consistent under localization.
Feasible recovery is asymptotically complete along boxes containing a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U_k-\underline L_k\to0.

notation.meaning: Minimum valid lower bound over live nodes.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Convergence of Fair Bilinear Spatial Refinement

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Introduce \(w\) for \(xy\). Initialize with the four McCormick inequalities on \([\ell_x,u_x]\times[\ell_y,u_y]\). Solve the resulting convex relaxation, choose a box containing a nonzero residual \(|w-xy|\), and bisect one of its variable intervals. Recompute the McCormick inequalities on each child box and repeat. A node may stop when it is infeasible, dominated by an incumbent, or satisfies a prescribed residual and optimality tolerance. The output is the best feasible incumbent; under exhaustive nested refinement with box diameters tending to zero, the relaxations converge to the bilinear graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded bilinear terms admit McCormick relaxations that converge to the exact graph under exhaustive spatial partitioning.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General bilinear program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The mixed term is a source of nonconvexity, but the stated assumptions alone do not guarantee that the objective is neither convex nor concave: degeneracy can occur when the coupling vanishes or is affine on the feasible affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bilinear program has the form \[\min_{x\in X,\,y\in Y} f(x,y)=\langle p,x\rangle+x^{T}Cy+\langle q,y\rangle,\] where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) are nonempty polyhedra, \(C\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), \(p\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(q\in\mathbb R^m\). The coupling term \(x^TCy\) generally makes the objective neither convex nor concave on \(X\times Y\), subject to the stated degeneracy boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilinear program minimizes a linear-plus-bilinear objective over two nonempty polyhedra. A nondegenerate bilinear coupling generally makes the objective neither convex nor concave, although this does not follow unconditionally when the coupling or feasible affine hull is degenerate.
assumptions_latex: X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ and }Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\text{ are nonempty polyhedra}
C\in\mathbb R^{n\times m},\quad p\in\mathbb R^n,\quad q\in\mathbb R^m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in X,\,y\in Y}\{\langle p,x\rangle+x^TCy+\langle q,y\rangle\}\text{ is a bilinear program; nondegenerate coupling generally destroys both convexity and concavity.}

knowledge_statements.title: DC Reduction Routes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph lifting of a DC objective into concave minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb{R}:g(x)\leq t\leq U\}\). This set is compact and convex. The lifted objective \(t-h(x)\) is concave because it is affine in \(t\) and \(-h\) is concave. For any fixed \(x\), minimization over feasible \(t\) selects \(t=g(x)\). Therefore the DC problem \(\min_{x\in C}\{g(x)-h(x)\}\) and the concave-minimization problem \(\min_{(x,t)\in E}\{t-h(x)\}\) have equal optimal values, and their optimal solutions correspond under projection onto \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epigraph lifting converts a continuous DC objective into an equivalent concave objective over a compact convex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in C}(g(x)-h(x))=\min_{(x,t)\in E}(t-h(x))\)

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compact-Lift Boundary for the DC Epigraph Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes value equivalence from the compact convex formulation required by the stated concave-minimization route.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(E_U=\{(x,t):x\in C,\ g(x)\le t\le U\}\), every \(x\in C\) has a lifted representative if and only if \(U\ge\sup_{x\in C}g(x)\). If no finite such \(U\) exists, this construction cannot produce a compact lifted feasible set. Omitting \(t\le U\) preserves \(\inf_{x\in C}(g(x)-h(x))\) through minimization over \(t\), but the resulting epigraph is generally noncompact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite uniform upper bound on the first convex component is necessary for this route to produce a compact lift, although the untruncated epigraph still preserves the infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\forall x\in C)(\exists t:(x,t)\in E_U)\iff U\ge\sup_{x\in C}g(x)
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Lift Boundary for the DC Epigraph Route

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scalar bilinear decomposition into two convex quadratics.

source_refs.locator: 9.3.1 Biconvex and Convex-Concave Programming p. 190

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(g(x,y)=\frac14(x+y)^2\) and \(h(x,y)=\frac14(x-y)^2\). Both \(g\) and \(h\) are convex quadratic functions on \(\mathbb{R}^2\), and direct expansion yields \(xy=g(x,y)-h(x,y)\). Thus every scalar bilinear term has an exact difference-of-convex representation. For vectors, a finite sum of bilinear terms is represented by summing these component decompositions, with coefficient signs absorbed by interchanging the two convex components when necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every bilinear term is exactly the difference of two convex quadratic functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear-to-DC Interfaces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative complementarity represented by one bilinear equality.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonnegative vectors, each product \(a_jb_j\) is nonnegative. Consequently, the componentwise conditions \(a_jb_j=0\) for all \(j\) are equivalent to the single equality \(\psi(a,b)=\sum_{j=1}^q a_jb_j=0\). Equivalently, since \(\psi(a,b)\geq0\), they may be imposed by \(\psi(a,b)\leq0\). This reduction replaces a complementarity system by a bilinear nonconvex constraint without changing its feasible set; bounded instances may subsequently be treated through bilinear relaxations or DC decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under nonnegativity, componentwise complementarity is equivalent to one equality setting the sum of all pairwise products to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity Reductions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonnegativity Is Essential for Aggregate Complementarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp cancellation failure for the aggregate-product equality when signed components are permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a=(1,1)\) and \(b=(1,-1)\). Then \(\sum_{j=1}^2a_jb_j=0\), although \(a_1b_1=1\ne0\) and \(a_2b_2=-1\ne0\). Thus the aggregate equality does not imply componentwise zero products without termwise nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Signed product terms can cancel, so a zero aggregate sum need not enforce componentwise complementarity.
assumptions_latex: \(a,b\in\mathbb R^2\) are not restricted to the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{j=1}^2a_jb_j=0\not\Rightarrow (\forall j)\ a_jb_j=0
knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegativity Is Essential for Aggregate Complementarity

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The extreme points of \(P_d\) are exactly the binary vectors \(\{0,1\}^d\), so \(|\operatorname{ext}(P_d)|=2^d\). A concave function on a compact polytope has a global minimizer at an extreme point, but an algorithm that realizes this fact by explicitly generating and evaluating every extreme point performs \(N_d=2^d\) point generations and objective evaluations on \(P_d\). Thus the enumeration resource grows exponentially with dimension even though the hypercube itself has only \(2d\) facet inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dimension-d hypercube has 2^d vertices, so full extreme-point enumeration requires exponentially many generations and evaluations.
knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Point Enumeration Growth

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The ball \(B_d\) is compact and convex, and every point of its boundary sphere \(S^{d-1}=\{x:\|x\|_2=1\}\) is extreme; no interior point is extreme. Hence \(\operatorname{ext}(B_d)=S^{d-1}\), an uncountable set. Although \(f\) has a global minimizer at an extreme point, the polyhedral strategy of listing all vertices has no finite analogue on \(B_d\). The extreme-point optimality principle therefore remains valid, while exhaustive finite enumeration fails when polyhedrality is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Euclidean ball has uncountably many extreme points, so the extreme-point principle does not yield a finite enumeration method.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonpolyhedral Geometry Limits

knowledge_statements.title: General Concave-Minimization Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: NP-hardness through concave quadratic minimization over a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(L\succeq0\), the quadratic function \(q(x)=-x^\mathsf{T}Lx\) is concave. Its minimum over \([-1,1]^{|V|}\) is attained at a vertex \(s\in\{-1,1\}^{|V|}\). For such a sign vector, \(\frac14s^\mathsf{T}Ls\) equals the weight of the cut encoded by \(s\). Therefore \(\min_{x\in[-1,1]^{|V|}}q(x)=-4\operatorname{MaxCut}(G)\). Computing the global minimum of a concave quadratic over a box is consequently NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted MAX-CUT reduces exactly to minimizing a concave quadratic over a box, establishing NP-hardness of this restricted concave-minimization family.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is an undirected graph with nonnegative rational edge weights.
\(L\) is the weighted Laplacian of \(G\), using the convention \(x^\mathsf{T}Lx=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in[-1,1]^{|V|}}-x^\mathsf{T}Lx=-4\operatorname{MaxCut}(G)\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC functions and DC programming problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines both a difference-of-convex function and the general constrained DC optimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. A real-valued function \(g\) is DC on \(C\) if there exist convex functions \(p,q:C\to\mathbb R\) such that \(g(x)=p(x)-q(x)\) for every \(x\in C\). A general DC program is \[\min_{x\in C} g(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad h_j(x)\le 0,\quad j=1,\ldots,m,\] where \(C\) is nonempty and convex and \(g,h_1,\ldots,h_m\) are DC on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function on a convex set is difference-of-convex when it is the difference of two convex functions. A general DC program minimizes a DC objective over a nonempty convex domain subject to finitely many DC inequality constraints.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and convex}
g,h_j:C\to\mathbb R\text{ are DC on }C\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,m

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual methods for reverse-convex programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition through the dual DC feasibility condition or the equivalent quasiconcave dual problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a DC feasibility problem governed by \(D(\gamma)\subset C\), the associated dual feasibility condition is \(C^*\subset [D(\gamma)]^*\). A method that solves the reverse-convex problem by solving this dual feasibility subproblem, or by solving the associated quasiconcave minimization problem over a convex set, is called a dual method. Solving the quasiconcave dual problem is equivalent to solving the original reverse-convex program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual method solves a reverse-convex program through the polar-set feasibility inclusion or the equivalent quasiconcave minimization problem over a convex set. Such a dual approach may operate in a lower-dimensional space than the primal approach.
assumptions_latex: \(D(\gamma)\subset C\) is the primal DC feasibility formulation under consideration.
The associated quasiconcave dual formulation exists as stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^*\subset [D(\gamma)]^*\) is the dual feasibility subproblem, and solving the associated quasiconcave dual problem is equivalent to solving the reverse-convex program.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cone-Splitting Restart Algorithm for LRC
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded initialization, restart phases, and terminal outcomes of the CS algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Solve \(\min\{cx\mid x\in D\}\) for a basic optimal solution \(w\). If \(h(w)\ge-\varepsilon\), terminate with \(w\) as an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate optimal solution. Otherwise, use an available vertex \(z^0\) satisfying \(h(z^0)>-\varepsilon\) to enter Phase 1, or set \(\gamma=+\infty\) and \(D(\gamma)=D\) and enter Phase 2. In Phase 1, search from \(z^0\) for \(\bar x\in X_{\varepsilon}\), set \(\gamma=c\bar x\) and \(D(\gamma)=\{x\in D\mid cx\le\gamma\}\), and proceed to Phase 2. In Phase 2, apply Procedure DC with \(D(\gamma),C_{\varepsilon},C_{\eta}\). If it produces \(z\in D(\gamma)\setminus C_{\varepsilon}\), set \(z^0\leftarrow z\) and restart Phase 1. If it establishes \(D(\gamma)\subset C_{\eta}\), terminate with \(\bar x\) as an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate optimal solution when \(\gamma<+\infty\), or declare \((\mathrm{LRC})\) infeasible when \(\gamma=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method solves the host linear program, searches for an approximate feasible incumbent when necessary, and applies Procedure DC on the incumbent sublevel set. A point outside the epsilon set triggers a restart; containment in the eta set yields approximate optimality when an incumbent exists and infeasibility otherwise.
assumptions_latex: \(w\text{ is a basic optimal solution of }\min\{cx\mid x\in D\}.\)
\(D(\gamma),C_{\varepsilon},C_{\eta}\text{ are the sets used by Procedure DC in the stated LRC construction}.\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{At a stated termination test, the algorithm returns an }\varepsilon\text{-approximate solution or declares }(\mathrm{LRC})\text{ infeasible; otherwise it restarts}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reverse-convex inequalities and linear reverse-convex programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the model family and records its principal geometric and complexity boundary; illustrative reformulations are omitted from the core definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reverse-convex inequality has the form $h(x)\ge 0$, where $h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is convex. A linear reverse-convex program has the form $\min\{c^Tx:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0,\ h(x)\ge0\}$. The reverse-convex constraint can destroy convexity and connectedness of the feasible set, and testing feasibility is NP-hard even when $h$ is a convex quadratic function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reverse-convex inequality requires a convex function to be nonnegative. Adding such an inequality to a linear program can make its feasible set nonconvex or disconnected, and feasibility is NP-hard even for a convex quadratic constraint function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{c^Tx:x\in D,\ h(x)\ge0\}\text{ is a linear reverse-convex program; its feasibility problem is NP-hard even for convex quadratic }h.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conical Branch-and-Bound Algorithm for LRC
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded initialization, cone bounding, incumbent updating, pruning, termination, and branching rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Solve \(\min\{cx\mid x\in D\}\) for a basic optimal solution \(w\). If \(h(w)\ge-\varepsilon\), terminate with \(w\) as an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate optimal solution. Otherwise obtain \(\bar x^1\in X_{\varepsilon}\) and set \(\gamma_1=c\bar x^1\) when the Phase 1 search is available; otherwise set \(\gamma_1=+\infty\) and \(D(\gamma_1)=D\). Initialize the cone net with the canonical cone \(M_0\) at \(x^0=w\). At iteration \(k\), solve LP (7.53) for each cone newly requiring a bound, obtaining \(\beta(M)\), \(\bar t(M)\), and \(\omega(M)=x^0+U\bar t(M)\). Optionally improve the incumbent using a feasible \(\omega(M)\) with objective below \(\gamma_k\). Prune every cone with \(\beta(M)\ge\gamma_k\). If no cone remains, terminate with the current incumbent as an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate optimal solution when \(\gamma_k<+\infty\), or declare \((\mathrm{LRC})\) infeasible when \(\gamma_k=+\infty\). Otherwise select a remaining cone of minimum \(\beta(M)\), subdivide it along the halfline from \(x^0\) through its point \(\omega(M)\), replace that cone by the resulting partition in the net, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm maintains an incumbent and a partition into cones. It computes a linear-programming lower bound for each relevant cone, prunes cones that cannot improve the incumbent, terminates with approximate optimality or infeasibility when the net is exhausted, and otherwise splits a cone having minimum lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(w\text{ is a basic optimal solution of }\min\{cx\mid x\in D\}.\)
\(M_0\text{ is the canonical cone associated with }x^0=w.\)
\(\beta(M),\bar t(M),\omega(M)\text{ are obtained from LP }(7.53)\text{ for the relevant cones}.\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{At a stated termination test, the method returns an }\varepsilon\text{-approximate solution or declares infeasibility; otherwise it refines the cone net}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cone-Wise LP Lower Bound and Edge Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded lower bound for an LRC restriction to a cone, with a sufficient exactness condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(S=D\setminus\operatorname{int}C\), the optimal value \(\beta(M)\) of
\[\min\left\{\left\langle c,x^0+Ut\right\rangle\ \middle|\ \widetilde A Ut\le\widetilde b,\ \sum_{i=1}^n\frac{t_i}{\theta_i}\ge1,\ t\ge0\right\}\]
is a lower bound for \(\min\{cx\mid x\in D\cap M,\ h(x)\ge0\}\). If a basic optimal solution \(\bar t(M)\) gives \(\omega(M)=x^0+U\bar t(M)\) lying on an edge of \(M\), then \(\omega(M)\in S\) and \(\beta(M)=\min\{cx\mid x\in M\cap S\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The displayed linear program gives a lower bound on the reverse-convex problem restricted to a cone. If its basic optimizer maps to an edge of the cone, the mapped point is feasible and the bound is exact over that cone.
assumptions_latex: \(\beta(M)\text{ is the optimal value of the displayed linear program}.\)
\(\bar t(M)\text{ is a basic optimal solution and }\omega(M)=x^0+U\bar t(M).\)
\(\omega(M)\text{ lies on an edge of }M\text{ for the exactness conclusion}.\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\beta(M)\le\min\{cx\mid x\in D\cap M,\ h(x)\ge0\}\), and under the edge condition, \(\omega(M)\in S\) and \(\beta(M)=\min\{cx\mid x\in M\cap S\}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularity of a linear reverse-convex program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the extract's unambiguous neighborhood definition; its printed closure identity is inconsistent with that formulation and is therefore not asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The problem is regular (stable) if, for every feasible $x$ and every neighborhood $U$ of $x$, there exists a feasible $x'\in U$ such that $h(x')>0$. Thus feasible points, including boundary points, can be approximated by points satisfying the reverse-convex inequality strictly; an isolated feasible point fails this condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear reverse-convex problem is regular when every feasible point can be approached arbitrarily closely by feasible points satisfying the reverse-convex constraint strictly. In particular, an isolated feasible point makes the problem nonregular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in S\ \forall U\ni x\ \exists x'\in U\cap S:\ h(x')>0.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A single reverse-convex constraint model is an optimization problem of the form \(\min\{f(x):x\in C,\ g(x)\geq0\}\), where \(C\) is convex and \(g\) is convex. Its feasible set is \(F=C\cap\{x:g(x)\geq0\}=C\setminus\{x:g(x)<0\}\). The excluded strict sublevel set \(\{x\in C:g(x)<0\}\) is convex, whereas its complement in \(C\) need not be convex. The adjective “single” refers to the presence of exactly one such convex exclusion function, irrespective of the number of inequalities used to describe \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A multiple reverse-convex constraint model has feasible set
\[
F=\{x\in P:g_i(x)\geq0\text{ for every }i=1,\ldots,m\}.
\]
For each \(i\), define the convex exclusion
\[
C_i=\{x\in P:g_i(x)<0\}.
\]
The model equivalently retains the points of \(P\) outside every exclusion:
\[
F=P\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus C_i)=P\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiple reverse-convex model retains the points of a convex base region that satisfy every convex inequality in the reverse direction, equivalently excluding a finite union of convex strict sublevel sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Reverse-Convex Constraint Models

source_refs.locator: 1.9 Polyhedral Convex Sets p. 27

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_j^\top x<b_j\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,q\}.
\]
Then
\[
\mathbb{R}^n\setminus C=\bigcup_{j=1}^q\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_j^\top x\geq b_j\}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
P\setminus C=P\cap\bigcup_{j=1}^q\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_j^\top x\geq b_j\},
\]
so membership outside the exclusion is certified by the failure of at least one strict defining inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complement of an open polyhedron is a finite union of closed halfspaces, so a point lies outside the exclusion exactly when at least one strict defining inequality fails.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strictness Determines the Complement Branches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary convention for polyhedral exclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C_{\rm cl}=\{x:a_j^\top x\le b_j,\ j=1,\ldots,q\}\), then \[\mathbb R^n\setminus C_{\rm cl}=\bigcup_{j=1}^q\{x:a_j^\top x>b_j\}.\] Thus replacing strict defining inequalities by non-strict inequalities changes the complementary branches from closed to open halfspaces and changes boundary feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed polyhedral exclusion has open complementary branches; the closed-halfspace complement formula for an open exclusion cannot be reused unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(C_{\rm cl}\) is defined by finitely many non-strict affine inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb R^n\setminus C_{\rm cl}=\bigcup_j\{x:a_j^\top x>b_j\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-of-Affine Defining Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent scalar representation of an open polyhedral exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x:a_j^\top x<b_j,\ j=1,\ldots,q\}\) and define \(g(x)=\max_{1\le j\le q}(a_j^\top x-b_j)\). Then \(g\) is polyhedral convex and \[C=\{x:g(x)<0\},\qquad \mathbb R^n\setminus C=\{x:g(x)\ge0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An open polyhedron is the strict sublevel set of the maximum of its affine defining residuals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\{g<0\}\) for \(g(x)=\max_j(a_j^\top x-b_j)\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is open and convex, \(\partial C\cap U\subseteq\{x\in U:g(x)=0\}\), and the gradient supplies first-order boundary geometry at zero-level points.

source_refs.locator: 2.2 Convex and Concave Functions p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A smooth convex exclusion is the nonempty strict sublevel set
\[
C=\{x\in U:g(x)<0\},
\]
where \(g\) is convex and continuously differentiable on the open convex set \(U\). The set \(C\) is open and convex, and continuity gives
\[
\partial C\cap U\subseteq\{x\in U:g(x)=0\}.
\]
At any \(\bar x\in U\) satisfying \(g(\bar x)=0\), convexity gives
\[
g(y)\geq\nabla g(\bar x)^\top(y-\bar x)\quad\text{for every }y\in U.
\]
In particular, every \(y\in C\) satisfies \(\nabla g(\bar x)^\top(y-\bar x)<0\), which supplies affine supporting geometry for the exclusion boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth convex exclusion is a nonempty strict sublevel set of a continuously differentiable convex function on an open convex domain. Its boundary lies on the zero level, where the gradient supplies affine supporting geometry.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Convex Exclusions

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2 Convex and Concave Functions p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\). Then \(g\) is continuously differentiable and convex, \(g(0)=0\), and \(\nabla g(0)=0\), but \(\{x:g(x)<0\}=\varnothing\). Hence a zero-level point need not have a nonzero supporting gradient when nonemptiness of the strict sublevel is omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function x squared has an empty negative sublevel and zero gradient at its zero-level point, showing why nonemptiness is essential.
assumptions_latex: The nonemptiness assumption on \(\{g<0\}\) is omitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(0)=0\) and \(\nabla g(0)=0\) although \(g\) is smooth and convex.
