assumptions_latex: \(g:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite and convex but need not be differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is open and convex, and each \(s\in\partial g(\bar x)\) satisfies \(g(y)\geq g(\bar x)+s^\top(y-\bar x)\) for every \(y\in U\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of g at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty finite convex exclusions whose boundary geometry is described by subgradients.

source_refs.locator: 2.2 Convex and Concave Functions p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonsmooth convex exclusion is the nonempty strict sublevel set
\[
C=\{x\in U:g(x)<0\}
\]
of a finite convex function \(g\) on an open convex set \(U\), without requiring differentiability. For \(\bar x\in U\), its convex subdifferential is
\[
\partial g(\bar x)=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:g(y)\geq g(\bar x)+s^\top(y-\bar x)\text{ for every }y\in U\}.
\]
If \(g(\bar x)=0\), then every \(s\in\partial g(\bar x)\) satisfies
\[
s^\top(y-\bar x)<0\quad\text{for every }y\in C,
\]
so the subgradients describe affine supporting directions for the exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsmooth convex exclusion is a nonempty convex strict sublevel set on an open convex domain. Its first-order supporting geometry is represented by the convex subdifferential rather than a unique gradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Convex Exclusions

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2 Convex and Concave Functions p. 35

assumptions_latex: The reverse-convex program minimizes \(f(x)\) over \(x\in P\) subject to \(g_i(x)\geq0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each reverse-convex constraint has the exact DC form \(0-g_i(x)\leq0\), while the objective has the DC form \(f(x)-0\); the feasible set and objective values are unchanged.

notation.meaning: generic difference of two convex functions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact difference-of-convex encoding of reverse-convex inequalities.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3
7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The reverse-convex program
\[
\min\{f(x):x\in P,\ g_i(x)\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}
\]
has the exact difference-of-convex formulation
\[
\min\{f(x)-0:x\in P,\ 0-g_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}.
\]
In each displayed difference, both components are convex. The reformulation preserves objective values, feasible points, and global minimizers; it changes only the algebraic representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every reverse-convex inequality with a convex left-hand side is exactly a difference-of-convex inequality, obtained by writing zero minus the convex function as at most zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical DC Reformulations

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3
7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical DC Encoding Does Not Convexify
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representational rather than convexifying character of the canonical DC route.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g(x)=x^2-1\), the reverse-convex constraint \(g(x)\ge0\) is exactly the canonical DC inequality \(0-g(x)\le0\), but its feasible set is \(( -\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\), which is nonconvex. Thus exact DC encoding alone neither convexifies the feasible set nor supplies a convex relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Writing a reverse-convex inequality in DC form preserves its nonconvex feasible set; it is an algebraic reformulation, not a convexification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:0-g(x)\le0\}=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\) is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical DC Encoding Does Not Convexify

assumptions_latex: The aggregate set \(C=\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i=P\setminus C\), so the aggregate \(C\) gives an exact single convex-exclusion representation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact aggregation when the union of the specified exclusions remains convex.

source_refs.locator: 7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a multiple-exclusion model have feasible set
\[
F=P\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i.
\]
If the aggregate set
\[
C=\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i
\]
is convex, then
\[
F=P\setminus C,
\]
which is an exact single convex-exclusion representation. Without convexity of this aggregate set, the set identity remains true, but this particular aggregate does not in general define a single convex exclusion of the same model class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the union of the specified convex exclusions is itself convex, their aggregate gives an exact single-exclusion representation. Without that hypothesis, the same union still represents the removed set but generally is not one convex exclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-to-Single Exclusion Reductions

source_witnesses.locator: 7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Union of Convex Exclusions Need Not Be Convex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of direct multiple-to-single aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R\), let \(C_1=(-2,0)\) and \(C_2=(0,2)\). Both exclusions are open and convex, but \(C_1\cup C_2=(-2,0)\cup(0,2)\) is not convex because it contains \(-1\) and \(1\) but not their midpoint \(0\). Hence direct aggregation does not generally remain in the single-convex-exclusion model class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two convex exclusions can have a nonconvex union, so direct aggregation into one convex exclusion requires the convex-union hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_1\cup C_2\) is not convex.
knowledge_statements.title: A Union of Convex Exclusions Need Not Be Convex

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\operatorname{proj}_x\widehat F\), where \(\widehat F=\{(x,y)\in P\times Y:h_j(x,y)\geq0\text{ for every }j=1,\ldots,r\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact extended formulations whose projection recovers the specified original feasible set.

source_refs.locator: 8. Dual Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A projection-based reverse-convex representation of \(F\subseteq P\) is an extended set
\[
\widehat F=\{(x,y)\in P\times Y:h_j(x,y)\geq0\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,r\}
\]
satisfying
\[
F=\operatorname{proj}_x\widehat F=\{x\in P:\exists y\in Y\text{ such that }(x,y)\in\widehat F\}.
\]
Exactness comprises both inclusions: every lifted feasible pair projects into \(F\), and every \(x\in F\) admits at least one feasible lift \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projection-based representation introduces auxiliary variables and convex functions used in reverse-convex inequalities so that projecting the lifted feasible set onto the original variables gives exactly the specified feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Based Representations

source_witnesses.locator: 8. Dual Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 181

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is polyhedral and \(C\subseteq P\) is convex.
\(Q\subseteq P\) is a polyhedron satisfying \(C\subseteq Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\setminus Q\subseteq P\setminus C\), so annexing \(Q\) yields a valid inner representation of the reverse-convex feasible region.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid inner representations obtained by covering an exclusion with an annexed polyhedron.

source_refs.locator: 10.2 Polyhedral Annexation p. 99
8.1 Polyhedral Annexation Method p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given the reverse-convex feasible region \(F=P\setminus C\), choose a polyhedral annex \(Q\) with
\[
C\subseteq Q\subseteq P.
\]
Then the residual polyhedral set
\[
F_Q=P\setminus Q
\]
is a valid inner representation because \(F_Q\subseteq F\). If \(Q=C\), the representation is exact; otherwise it deliberately removes the additional region \(Q\setminus C\). A sequence of annexes \(Q_k\supseteq C\) approaching \(C\) produces increasingly accurate residual representations when the associated set convergence is established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Covering a convex exclusion by a polyhedron and removing that polyhedron gives a valid inner feasible region; exactness holds only when the annex equals the exclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral-Annexation Representations

source_witnesses.locator: 10.2 Polyhedral Annexation p. 99
8.1 Polyhedral Annexation Method p. 181

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited local material is only a table of contents and does not establish that polyhedral annexation means covering an exclusion C by a polyhedron Q and replacing the feasible region by P\Q. Moreover, the statement incorrectly calls P\Q a polyhedral set: the relative complement of one polyhedron in another is generally a finite union of polyhedra, not a polyhedron. Because the exact annexation convention and resulting representation cannot be recovered reliably from the available source, authoritative full-text support is required.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\setminus C=\bigcup_{j=1}^q\bigl(P\cap\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_j^\top x\geq b_j\}\bigr)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite disjunctive representation of the complement of an open polyhedral exclusion.

source_refs.locator: 1.9 Polyhedral Convex Sets p. 27
7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the open polyhedral exclusion
\[
C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_j^\top x<b_j\text{ for every }j=1,\ldots,q\},
\]
define
\[
D_j=P\cap\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_j^\top x\geq b_j\}.
\]
De Morgan's law gives the exact finite disjunction
\[
P\setminus C=\bigcup_{j=1}^q D_j.
\]
Thus a point is feasible precisely when it belongs to at least one branch, equivalently when at least one strict inequality defining the exclusion fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complement of an open polyhedral exclusion is exactly the union of branches obtained by reversing one defining strict inequality at a time.
knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Exclusion Representations

source_witnesses.locator: 1.9 Polyhedral Convex Sets p. 27
7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Halfspace Disjunction Requires Polyhedrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the finite reversed-affine-branch construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge2\), the complement of the open Euclidean unit ball \(B=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_2<1\}\) is not a finite union of closed halfspaces. Otherwise, taking complements would express \(B\) as a finite intersection of open halfspaces, contrary to its nonpolyhedral curved boundary. Thus the seed's finite halfspace-disjunction formula depends essentially on polyhedral exclusion geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exterior of a Euclidean ball is not a finite union of closed halfspaces, so the finite reversed-inequality construction does not extend to curved exclusions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb R^n\setminus B\) is not representable as a finite union of closed halfspaces.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Halfspace Disjunction Requires Polyhedrality

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex and compact, and \(C\subseteq P\) is nonempty, open relative to \(P\), and convex.
The unique minimizer \(x^0\) of \(f\) over \(P\) belongs to \(C\), and \(P\setminus C\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every minimizer \(x^*\) of \(f\) over \(P\setminus C\) lies in \(\partial_P C\).

notation.meaning: relative boundary of C in P

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary localization when the strictly convex objective's base-region minimizer is excluded.

source_refs.locator: 7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
\min\{f(x):x\in P\setminus C\}.
\]
Compactness and continuity ensure existence of a minimizer. If the unique minimizer \(x^0\) of \(f\) on \(P\) lies in the excluded set \(C\), then every global minimizer \(x^*\) of the reverse-convex problem satisfies
\[
x^*\in\partial_P C.
\]
Thus no reverse-convex minimizer can lie in the relative interior of \(P\setminus C\); optimality is localized to the boundary separating the excluded convex region from its feasible complement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a strictly convex objective's unique minimizer lies inside one convex exclusion, every minimizer remaining after that exclusion lies on its relative boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Exclusion Boundary Localization

source_witnesses.locator: 7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonexcluded Base Minimizer Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of boundary localization when the base-region minimizer remains feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=[-2,2]\), \(C=(1,2]\), and \(f(x)=x^2\). The unique minimizer of \(f\) on \(P\) is \(0\notin C\), and it remains the unique minimizer on \(P\setminus C=[-2,1]\), whereas \(\partial_P C=\{1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the base minimizer is not excluded, it can remain optimal away from the exclusion boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\setminus C}f=\{0\}\not\subseteq\partial_P C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Nonexcluded Base Minimizer Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict-Convexity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict convexity is needed to localize every optimizer rather than guarantee a boundary optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=[-2,2]\), \(C=(-1,1)\), and \(f\equiv0\), every point of \(P\setminus C\) is optimal, including points outside \(\partial_P C=\{-1,1\}\). Thus ordinary convexity does not localize every minimizer, although boundary minimizers still exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without strict convexity, boundary minimizers may coexist with optimal points away from the boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\setminus C}f=P\setminus C\not\subseteq\partial_P C\).

notation.meaning: relative boundary of C in P

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Convexity Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-Exclusion Attainment Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative openness of the exclusion ensures the retained complement is closed; dropping it can destroy attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=[-2,2]\), \(C=[-1,1]\), and \(f(x)=x^2\). The base minimizer \(0\) lies in \(C\), but \(P\setminus C=[-2,-1)\cup(1,2]\) has infimum \(1\) and no minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed exclusion can leave a nonclosed feasible complement on which the localized boundary infimum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in P\setminus C}f(x)=1\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\setminus C}f=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Exclusion Attainment Failure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-Objective Boundary-Minimizer Variant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weaker convex-objective variant guaranteeing existence, but not exclusivity, of a boundary optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P\) is compact and convex, \(C\subseteq P\) is nonempty, relatively open, and convex, and a continuous convex function \(f\) has a minimizer \(x^0\in C\), then whenever \(P\setminus C\neq\varnothing\), the minimum of \(f\) over \(P\setminus C\) is attained at some point of \(\partial_P C\). Other minimizers may lie away from that boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a merely convex objective whose base minimizer is excluded, at least one reverse-convex minimizer lies on the exclusion boundary, although not every minimizer need do so.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq P\) is nonempty, relatively open, and convex, with \(P\setminus C\neq\varnothing\).
\(f:P\to\mathbb R\) is continuous and convex and has a minimizer \(x^0\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\setminus C}f\cap\partial_P C\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: relative boundary of C in P

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Objective Boundary-Minimizer Variant

assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is open and convex, \(P\subseteq U\), and \(m\geq1\).
For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), \(g_i:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite and convex, and \(C_i=\{x\in U:g_i(x)<0\}\) is nonempty.
\(F=\{x\in P:g_i(x)\geq0\text{ for every }i=1,\ldots,m\}\), and \(\bar x\in F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active exclusion set is \(I(\bar x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:g_i(\bar x)=0\}\); these are exactly the indices whose boundaries contain \(\bar x\), and their subgradients supply supporting directions.

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of the ith exclusion function
strict convex exclusion induced by the ith function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local supporting geometry of nonempty exclusion boundaries active at a feasible point.

source_refs.locator: 2.2 Convex and Concave Functions p. 35
7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a feasible point \(\bar x\in F\), define
\[
I(\bar x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:g_i(\bar x)=0\}.
\]
Because each \(C_i\) is nonempty and each finite convex function \(g_i\) is continuous on \(U\), these are exactly the indices satisfying
\[
\bar x\in\partial C_i.
\]
For every \(i\in I(\bar x)\) and every \(s_i\in\partial g_i(\bar x)\), convexity yields
\[
g_i(y)\geq s_i^\top(y-\bar x)\quad\text{for every }y\in U.
\]
Hence every \(y\in C_i\) satisfies \(s_i^\top(y-\bar x)<0\). The active subgradients therefore record supporting geometry for all exclusion boundaries incident at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a feasible point, an exclusion is active when its convex defining function vanishes. For nonempty exclusions on an open convex domain, these are exactly the incident exclusion boundaries, and their subgradients provide supporting directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Active Exclusion Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2 Convex and Concave Functions p. 35
7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Irrelevance of Inactive Exclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood characterization showing that only active reverse-convex exclusions contribute incident boundary geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\) be finite convex functions on an open set \(U\), let \(F=\{x\in P:g_i(x)\geq0\ \forall i\}\), and fix \(\bar x\in F\). If \(j\notin I(\bar x)=\{i:g_i(\bar x)=0\}\), then \(g_j(\bar x)>0\). Continuity gives a neighborhood \(V_j\) of \(\bar x\) such that \(g_j(x)>0\) throughout \(V_j\). Because there are finitely many indices, there is one neighborhood \(V\) on which every inactive exclusion remains strictly satisfied. Consequently, only indices in \(I(\bar x)\) contribute exclusion boundaries incident at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every inactive reverse-convex constraint remains strictly satisfied near the point, so only active exclusions contribute incident boundary geometry.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_i:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite and convex, and there are finitely many indices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists V\ni\bar x\text{ such that }g_j(x)>0\quad\forall x\in V,\ \forall j\notin I(\bar x).

notation.meaning: indices of exclusions active at the feasible point
neighborhood on which every inactive exclusion remains strict

knowledge_statements.title: Local Irrelevance of Inactive Exclusions

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty open convex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(a^\top y<\beta\leq a^\top x\) for every \(y\in C\), then \(x\notin C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine separation certificates proving that a point lies outside an open convex exclusion.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Convex Sets p. 33

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A separation-based exclusion certificate for \(x\notin C\) is a pair \((a,\beta)\) satisfying
\[
a\neq0,\qquad a^\top y<\beta\text{ for every }y\in C,\qquad a^\top x\geq\beta.
\]
These inequalities place the entire open convex exclusion strictly in the halfspace
\[
\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:a^\top z<\beta\}
\]
and place \(x\) on the separating hyperplane or in the opposite closed halfspace. Consequently, the displayed data certify \(x\notin C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hyperplane certifies that a point is outside an open convex exclusion when every point of the exclusion lies strictly on one side while the tested point lies on the hyperplane or in the opposite closed halfspace.
knowledge_statements.title: Separation-Based Exclusion Certificates

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Convex Sets p. 33

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Requirement for Complete Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvex exclusions need not admit a single affine certificate for every exterior point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=B((-2,0),1)\cup B((2,0),1)\) and \(x=(0,0)\). Then \(C\) is open and \(x\notin C\), but \(x\in\operatorname{conv}C\); hence no \((a,\beta)\) satisfies \(a^\top y<\beta\leq a^\top x\) for every \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exterior point in the convex hull of a nonconvex exclusion may have no single affine certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\notin C\), but no seed-form affine certificate exists.

notation.meaning: open Euclidean ball of radius r centered at c

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Requirement for Complete Separation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Openness Requirement for Strict Pointwise Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A convex but nonopen exclusion may have a missing boundary point that admits no strict-on-every-point separator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(u,v):v>0\}\cup\{(u,0):u<0\}\) and \(x=(0,0)\). The set \(C\) is convex and \(x\notin C\). Any affine functional bounded above on the upper half-plane must have zero coefficient on \(u\); it then has equality at every point \((u,0)\in C\), so no certificate with \(a^\top y<\beta\leq a^\top x\) for every \(y\in C\) exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without openness, a missing boundary point of a convex set need not admit the certificate's strict pointwise separation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\notin C\), but no seed-form strict affine certificate exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Openness Requirement for Strict Pointwise Separation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Completeness of Affine Exclusion Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse characterizing nonmembership in a nonempty open convex exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, open, and convex, then every \(x\notin C\) admits \(a\neq0\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) such that \(a^\top y<\beta\leq a^\top x\) for all \(y\in C\). Thus seed-form certificates are sound and complete for point nonmembership.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point outside a nonempty open convex exclusion has a seed-form affine separation certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, open, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists a\neq0,\beta:\ a^\top y<\beta\leq a^\top x\ \forall y\in C.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Completeness of Affine Exclusion Certificates
Polyhedral Exclusion Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional vertex certificate for excluding a polytope contained in one forbidden convex region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g(v^j)<0\) for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\), then \(P\subseteq\{x\in X:g(x)<0\}\), and hence \(P\cap\{x\in X:g(x)\geq0\}=\varnothing\). The vertex list and inequalities \(g(v^j)<0\) constitute a polyhedral exclusion certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polytope is safely excluded when a convex reverse-constraint function is strictly negative at every vertex.
assumptions_latex: \(g:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex, and the reverse-convex constraint is \(g(x)\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\cap\{x\in X:g(x)\geq0\}=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex-Certificate Verification Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle cost of checking an explicitly listed polyhedral exclusion certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an explicit list of \(r\) vertices and oracle access to \(g\), verification of the certificate \(g(v^j)<0\) for all \(j\) requires \(r\) function evaluations and \(r\) strict-sign checks, apart from the cost of obtaining or validating the vertex list.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit r-vertex certificate is checked with r function evaluations and sign tests; vertex enumeration is a separate cost.
assumptions_latex: The \(r\) vertices of \(P\) are supplied explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{verification uses }r\text{ evaluations of }g\text{ and }O(r)\text{ sign checks}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Certificate Verification Cost

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Vertex-Margin Requirement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp sign boundary for excluding a polytope from a closed reverse-convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For feasibility \(g(x)\geq0\), inequalities \(g(v)\leq0\) at all vertices imply only \(g(x)\leq0\) on \(P=\operatorname{conv}V\). They do not certify disjointness from \(\{g\geq0\}\). For \(P=[-1,1]\) and \(g(x)=x^2-1\), both vertices have value zero and are feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonstrict vertex inequalities cannot exclude a cell from a closed reverse-convex feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}V\) is a polytope and \(g\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(v)\leq0\ \forall v\in V\not\Rightarrow P\cap\{g\geq0\}=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Vertex-Margin Requirement

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact and \(F=X\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:g_i(x)\geq0\}\), with every \(g_i\) convex.
A finite polyhedral partition of \(X\) and a valid lower-bounding rule for the objective are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At every iteration, \(F\subseteq O_{k+1}\subseteq O_k\subseteq X\); hence minimizing a valid relaxation over \(O_k\) gives a global lower bound.

notation.meaning: current outer approximation of the feasible set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested polyhedral outer approximation obtained by certified removal of infeasible cells.

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Outer Approximation Method p. 174

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(O_0=X\). At iteration \(k\), partition the unresolved portion of \(O_k\) into finitely many polytopes. Whenever a cell \(P\) has a certificate that \(P\subseteq\{x:g_i(x)<0\}\) for some \(i\), set \(O_{k+1}=O_k\setminus\operatorname{int}P\); otherwise retain or refine the cell. Compute a valid objective lower bound over the retained cells and an incumbent from reverse-convex feasible points. Stop when the smallest retained lower bound is no less than the incumbent within the prescribed tolerance; return that incumbent and the bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method maintains a nested polyhedral superset of the feasible set by removing only cells certified infeasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Reverse-Convex Outer Approximation

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Outer Approximation Method p. 174

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unsafe Pointwise Cell Deletion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A pointwise violation cannot replace a whole-cell infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=[-2,2]\), \(F=\{x\in X:x^2-1\geq0\}\), and \(f(x)=(x-3/2)^2\). The cell \(P=[0,2]\) contains the violating sample \(x=0\), but it also contains the unique global minimizer \(x^*=3/2\in F\). Deleting \(P\) merely because the sampled point violates the reverse-convex constraint removes the global optimizer. Safe deletion therefore requires a certificate that the entire deleted cell is disjoint from \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting a cell from one violating sample can remove its global optimizer; infeasibility must be certified over the whole cell.
assumptions_latex: The cell \(P=[0,2]\) is rejected solely from the violating sample \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\notin F\quad\text{but}\quad x^*=3/2\in P\cap F,\qquad f(x^*)=0.
knowledge_statements.title: Unsafe Pointwise Cell Deletion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence of Exhaustive Reverse-Convex Outer Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global convergence under exhaustive refinement, exclusion consistency, and consistent monotone regional bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) be compact, \(F\subseteq X\) be nonempty and closed, and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. Suppose finite retained-cell partitions define \(F\subseteq O_{k+1}\subseteq O_k\subseteq X\); only cells certified disjoint from \(F\) are deleted; every competitive infinite nested cell chain has diameter tending to zero and a limit in \(F\); and valid cell bounds are monotone under refinement and consistent, so \(P_j\downarrow\{x\}\) implies \(L(P_j)\to f(x)\). If competitive cells are processed fairly, then \(L_k:=\min_{P\in\mathcal P_k}L(P)\) increases to \(f^*:=\min_{x\in F}f(x)\). For every feasible incumbent value \(U_k\), termination with \(U_k-L_k\leq\varepsilon\) certifies that its incumbent is \(\varepsilon\)-globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Safe deletion, exhaustive vanishing-mesh refinement, exclusion consistency, and consistent monotone bounds make the global lower bound converge to the optimum; the incumbent gap is a global certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is compact, \(F\) is nonempty and closed, and \(f\) is continuous.
Only cells certified disjoint from \(F\) are deleted.
Every competitive retained nested chain is fairly refined to zero diameter and has its limit in \(F\).
Cell lower bounds are valid, monotone under refinement, and consistent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_k\uparrow f^*,\qquad U_k-L_k\leq\varepsilon\Longrightarrow U_k\leq f^*+\varepsilon.

notation.meaning: finite retained-cell partition at iteration k

knowledge_statements.title: Convergence of Exhaustive Reverse-Convex Outer Approximation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conical-subdivision algorithm for (LRCP)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A cut-split global algorithm using concavity-cut LP bounds, incumbent pruning, and bisection or solution-ray subdivision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R_+^n\), \(0\) is a vertex of \(\Omega\), and \(cx>0\) for every \(x\in\Omega\setminus\operatorname{int}C\). Initialize \(K_1=\mathbb R_+^n\), \(\mathcal S=\mathcal R=\{K_1\}\), and the best available feasible incumbent. For each \(K\in\mathcal S\), construct a concavity cut \(\ell_K(x)\ge0\) for \(K\setminus C\) and solve \(\min\{cx:x\in\Omega\cap K,\ell_K(x)\ge0\}\), obtaining a basic optimizer \(\omega(K)\) and bound \(\beta(K)\). Update the incumbent and delete every cone with \(\beta(K)\ge c\bar x\). If no cone remains, return \(\bar x\) as a global solution, or declare infeasibility if no incumbent exists. Otherwise select a remaining cone of minimum bound, subdivide it by bisection or along the ray through \(\omega(K)\), update the active collection, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm computes a concavity-cut LP bound on each active cone, prunes cones that cannot improve the incumbent, and subdivides a minimum-bound cone. Exhausting the active cones certifies global optimality or infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal R'=\varnothing\Rightarrow\left[(\bar x\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow\bar x\text{ solves }(LRCP))\land(\bar x=\varnothing\Rightarrow(LRCP)\text{ is infeasible})\right].

children.title: Reverse-Convex Cutting Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Cut constructions used to exclude reverse-convex infeasible regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Reverse-Convex Cutting Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cell-exclusion cuts based on convexity and vertex evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Select an index \(i\) and a polyhedral cell \(P=\operatorname{conv}V\) such that \(g_i(v)<0\) for every \(v\in V\). The resulting certificate gives \(P\subseteq\{x:g_i(x)<0\}\). Update the retained region by \(R\leftarrow R\setminus\operatorname{int}P\); this update preserves every point feasible for the full reverse-convex system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reverse-convex cutting mechanism removes a polyhedral cell only after its vertices certify that the entire cell violates one constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}V\subseteq X\) is a current polyhedral cell with finite vertex set \(V\).
\(g_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and defines the constraint \(g_i(x)\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update \(R\leftarrow R\setminus\operatorname{int}P\) preserves every point satisfying all reverse-convex constraints.

notation.meaning: finite vertex set of the cell

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mixed-Constraint Vertex Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why all vertices must violate the same convex reverse constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=[-1,1]\), \(g_1(x)=x\), and \(g_2(x)=-x\), with feasibility requiring both functions to be nonnegative. Vertex \(-1\) violates \(g_1\), and vertex \(1\) violates \(g_2\), but \(x=0\) is feasible. Thus vertex-dependent constraint indices cannot certify deletion of the cell.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different violated constraints at different vertices do not certify cell infeasibility; one common constraint must be negative at every vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl(\forall v\in\{-1,1\}\ \exists i:\ g_i(v)<0\bigr)\not\Rightarrow P\cap\{g_1\geq0,g_2\geq0\}=\varnothing.\)

children.top_down_role: Partition structures used to divide reverse-convex search regions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=P^-\cup P^+\), the child interiors are disjoint, and no point of \(P\) is lost.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\) so that both sides of \(H\) meet \(P\). Replace \(P\) by \(P^-=P\cap\{x:a^\top x\leq\beta\}\) and \(P^+=P\cap\{x:a^\top x\geq\beta\}\). Apply all exclusion and objective-bound tests independently to the children. Empty children are discarded; every nonempty child failing all fathoming tests enters the active set. The rule is lossless because \(P=P^-\cup P^+\), while refinement can make later convex-exclusion certificates decisive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unresolved polytope is split by a hyperplane into lossless child cells, which are then tested independently.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Longest-Side Box Bisection Variant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Axis-aligned lossless splitting with vanishing mesh under repeated midpoint longest-side selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(B=\prod_{j=1}^n[\ell_j,u_j]\), choose \(k\in\operatorname*{argmax}_j(u_j-\ell_j)\) and split the kth interval at its midpoint. The two closed child boxes cover \(B\), have disjoint interiors, and repeated longest-side midpoint bisection along an infinite nested branch yields diameters tending to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Midpoint bisection of a longest box side is lossless and produces zero-diameter refinement along every infinite branch.
assumptions_latex: Every continuing branch uses midpoint longest-side bisection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B=B^-\cup B^+\), \(\operatorname{int}B^-\cap\operatorname{int}B^+=\varnothing\), and \(\operatorname{diam}(B_k)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Longest-Side Box Bisection Variant

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exhaustive Refinement Condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness condition on repeated region splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A splitting regime is exhaustive when every parent is replaced by finitely many closed children covering it and every infinite nested branch \(P_0\supseteq P_1\supseteq\cdots\) satisfies \(\operatorname{diam}(P_k)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coverage-preserving finite splits are exhaustive when every infinite nested branch shrinks to zero diameter.
assumptions_latex: Every split has finitely many closed children covering the parent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall(P_k)\text{ generated along an infinite branch},\ \operatorname{diam}(P_k)\to0.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Exhaustive Refinement Condition

children.title: Cut–Split Coordination
children.top_down_role: Interfaces governing the interaction between cuts and regional splits.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut–Split Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordination invariant for alternating certified exclusion, bounding, and subdivision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Select \(P\in\mathcal A\). Discard \(P\) if a reverse-convex exclusion certificate applies or if \(L(P)\geq U-\varepsilon\). Otherwise search \(P\) for a feasible point and decrease \(U\) when one improves the incumbent. If \(P\) remains unresolved, split it into finitely many children whose union is \(P\), compute their valid lower bounds, and insert the unfathomed children into \(\mathcal A\). Stop when \(\mathcal A=\varnothing\) or \(U-\min_{Q\in\mathcal A}L(Q)\leq\varepsilon\); output the incumbent and its certified global gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut, bound, incumbent, and split operations are coordinated so that no feasible point capable of improving the incumbent beyond tolerance is lost.
assumptions_latex: The active list \(\mathcal A\) contains finitely described polyhedral cells covering every unresolved feasible point.
Every exclusion test and node lower bound used by the procedure is valid.
A feasible incumbent with finite value \(U\in\mathbb{R}\) is available, and \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active cells continue to cover every feasible point capable of improving the incumbent by more than \(\varepsilon\), and termination certifies the prescribed absolute global optimality gap.

notation.meaning: valid lower bound for cell P

children.title: Reverse-Convex Branching Regimes
children.top_down_role: Branching structures adapted to reverse-convex feasible geometry.

assumptions_latex: Each active node is a compact polyhedral cell, and branching replaces it by finitely many closed children covering it.
Along every infinite branch, the nested cell diameters tend to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every point retained indefinitely belongs to a nested branch of vanishing cells, so local consistency of bounds and exclusion tests can support exhaustive global search.

Node selection is fair when no node whose lower bound remains below the incumbent gap threshold is postponed forever. These coverage, refinement, and fairness predicates constitute a sufficient branching regime for spatially exhaustive reverse-convex search when paired with consistent node bounds.

children.title: Reverse-Convex Node Bounds
children.top_down_role: Regional bounds used within reverse-convex search trees.

assumptions_latex: The node cell \(P\) contains the local reverse-convex feasible set \(F_P\).
\(R(P)\) is a tractable relaxation satisfying \(F_P\subseteq R(P)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(P)=\inf_{x\in R(P)}\underline f_P(x)\leq\inf_{x\in F_P}f(x)\), so \(L(P)\) is a valid node lower bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation-based lower bounds for minimization nodes.

source_refs.locator: 7.3 Cut and Split (Branch and Bound) Methods p. 176

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\underline f_P:R(P)\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}\) satisfy \(\underline f_P(x)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in F_P\). Define \(L(P)=\inf_{x\in R(P)}\underline f_P(x)\). Because \(F_P\subseteq R(P)\), this quantity does not exceed the objective value of any reverse-convex feasible point in \(P\). Bounds are monotone under refinement when each child \(Q\subseteq P\) uses a relaxation and underestimator satisfying \(L(Q)\geq L(P)\); monotonicity is desirable but validity of the inequality is the essential requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node bound is valid when it minimizes an objective underestimator over a superset of that node's feasible points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active-Node Bound Aggregation with a Fathoming Cutoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global lower-bound certificate from valid node bounds and a certified lower cutoff on safely removed feasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal A be the active-node family and suppose every feasible point either lies in some P\in\mathcal A or has objective at least C, where C is a certified cutoff for safely removed points. If L(P) is valid on every active node, then L_{\mathrm{glob}}=\min\bigl(C,\inf_{P\in\mathcal A}L(P)\bigr) is a global lower bound, using \inf\varnothing=+\infty. For any verified feasible incumbent value U, U-L_{\mathrm{glob}}\le\varepsilon certifies epsilon-global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The least active-node bound and the certified cutoff for removed points combine into a global lower bound.
assumptions_latex: Every feasible point is active-node covered or has objective at least C.
Each L(P) is a valid node lower bound.
U is the value of a verified feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_{\mathrm{glob}}\le f^*\le U,\qquad U-L_{\mathrm{glob}}\le\varepsilon\Longrightarrow U\le f^*+\varepsilon.

children.title: Reverse-Convex Fathoming Criteria
children.top_down_role: Structural criteria for pruning reverse-convex search regions.

assumptions_latex: \(L(P)\) is a valid lower bound for node \(P\), and \(U\) is the value of a feasible incumbent.
\(\varepsilon\geq0\) is the accepted absolute optimality tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any node satisfying an exclusion, bound, or exact-resolution certificate may be removed without losing an \(\varepsilon\)-improving feasible solution.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A node \(P\) is safely fathomed if at least one verifiable condition holds: \(P\) has no reverse-convex feasible point; \(L(P)\geq U-\varepsilon\); or the node has been solved exactly and all its feasible points have objective at least \(U-\varepsilon\). Infeasibility may be certified by polyhedral exclusion or another valid constraint certificate. Bound fathoming certifies that no point in \(P\) can improve the incumbent by more than \(\varepsilon\). Exact-resolution fathoming additionally permits updating \(U\) before deleting the node.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node is fathomed by certified infeasibility, an incumbent-dominated lower bound, or exact resolution of its local problem.

assumptions_latex: Every processed node creates at most \(b\geq2\) children.
The search tree is truncated after depth \(d\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tree contains at most \(1+b+\cdots+b^d=(b^{d+1}-1)/(b-1)\) nodes and at most \(b^d\) depth-\(d\) cells.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rooted reverse-convex search tree with branching factor at most \(b\), level \(k\) contains at most \(b^k\) nodes. Consequently, generation through depth \(d\) requires at most \(N_d=\sum_{k=0}^d b^k=(b^{d+1}-1)/(b-1)\) node constructions, bound evaluations, and fathoming tests, up to constant multiplicities per node. This is a worst-case bound: exclusion and bound fathoming can reduce actual growth, but without such pruning exponential growth in \(d\) is attainable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-arity reverse-convex search tree can still grow exponentially with depth when fathoming is ineffective.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Primal Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hybrid primal scheme combining outer approximation, local feasible search, cutting, and branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\mathcal A\) with the compact initial region and set \(U=+\infty\). Repeatedly select a node, apply valid outer-approximation or polyhedral-exclusion cuts, search for a point feasible for the original constraints, update \(U\) from any improving feasible point, and compute valid node lower bounds. Fathom a node when it is certified infeasible or its lower bound is at least \(U-\varepsilon\); otherwise split it and insert its unfathomed children. When \(\mathcal A\neq\varnothing\), define \(L=\min_{P\in\mathcal A}L(P)\) and stop with an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal incumbent if \(U<+\infty\) and \(U-L\leq\varepsilon\). If \(\mathcal A=\varnothing\), return the incumbent as globally optimal when \(U<+\infty\), and otherwise report certified infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A combined primal method alternates exclusion, feasible search, bounding, and branching, returning a certified incumbent when the global gap closes or reporting infeasibility when exhaustive search finds none.
assumptions_latex: The reverse-convex problem has a compact initial region and valid exclusion, bounding, and branching procedures.
Every candidate incumbent is checked against the original constraints.
\(\varepsilon\geq0\) is the accepted absolute optimality tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If a feasible incumbent \(x^*\) is returned at finite-gap termination, then \(f(x^*)-f^*\leq\varepsilon\); exhaustion of the active set instead yields global optimality or certified infeasibility according to whether a finite incumbent exists.

Suppose safe fathoming and lossless branching preserve coverage; child bounds do not fall below their parent bound; every competitive infinite branch is processed and has diameters tending to zero; along every processed nested branch converging to x\in F, node bounds converge to f(x) and feasible search generates values converging to f(x); and every branch converging outside F is eventually certified infeasible or has bounds eventually exceeding every fixed number below f^*=\min_Ff. Then, for an infinite execution with nonempty active sets, the least active-node bound L_k and best verified feasible value U_k satisfy L_k\to f^*, U_k\to f^*, and U_k-L_k\to0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Combined conical-subdivision and outer-approximation algorithm for (CDC)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined reverse-convex primal method, including finite termination certificates and the normal-subdivision infinite-run guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume (48) and \(0\in\operatorname{int}\Omega\). Start with a polytope \(P_1\supset\Omega\) and cones covering \(P_1\), or at least a region known to contain a global optimizer. On each active cone \(K\), construct its concavity cut and solve \(\min\{cx:x\in P_k\cap K,\ell_K(x)\ge0\}\), obtaining \(\omega(K)\) and \(\beta(K)\). Update the incumbent and prune cones whose bounds cannot improve it. If no cone remains, return the incumbent as globally optimal, or declare infeasibility if no incumbent exists. Otherwise choose a minimum-bound cone and set \(x^k=\omega(K^*)\). If \(x^k\notin\Omega\), add a subgradient outer-approximation cut at \(y^k\in[0,x^k]\cap\partial\Omega\); then bisect or \(\omega\)-subdivide \(K^*\) and repeat. Under a normal subdivision rule, if the algorithm is infinite, at least one cluster point \(\widetilde x\) of \(\{x^k\}\) belongs to \(\Omega\cap\partial C\) and is a global optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This combined method computes cone-wise LP bounds, prunes using an incumbent, adds an outer-approximation cut when the selected LP point violates Omega, and subdivides the selected cone. Finite exhaustion certifies optimality or infeasibility; under normal subdivision, an infinite run has a globally optimal cluster point.
assumptions_latex: P_1\supset\Omega\text{, and the initial cones cover }P_1\text{ or a region known to contain a global optimizer}.
\text{A normal subdivision rule is used for the infinite-run conclusion.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal R'=\varnothing\Rightarrow\left[(\bar x\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow\bar x\text{ solves }(CDC))\land(\bar x=\varnothing\Rightarrow(CDC)\text{ is infeasible})\right];\quad\text{if the run is infinite under normal subdivision, }\exists\widetilde x\in\operatorname{cluster}(\{x^k\})\cap\Omega\cap\partial C\text{ globally optimal}.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact value-function projection of a two-block reverse-convex problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+m}\), let \(f:K\to\mathbb R\), and let \(h_i:K\to\mathbb R\) be convex for \(i=1,\ldots,r\). For each \(x\in X:=\operatorname{proj}_x K\), define \(Y(x):=\{y:(x,y)\in K,\ h_i(x,y)\geq0\text{ for every }i\}\) and \(v(x):=\inf_{y\in Y(x)}f(x,y)\), with \(v(x)=+\infty\) when \(Y(x)=\varnothing\). Then the reverse-convex problem has the exact projected representation \[\inf\{f(x,y):(x,y)\in K,\ h_i(x,y)\geq0\ \forall i\}=\inf_{x\in X}v(x).\] If an outer minimizer and its inner minimizer exist, their pair is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating one variable block through its exact conditional value function preserves the global optimal value and reconstructs global solutions when both minima are attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{(x,y)\in K,\ h(x,y)\geq0}f(x,y)=\inf_{x\in\operatorname{proj}_xK}v(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact decomposition by fixing a parameter block and solving conditional reverse-convex subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^p\), let \(K(\theta)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and let \(f_\theta:K(\theta)\to\mathbb R\) and convex functions \(h_{i,\theta}:K(\theta)\to\mathbb R\) be given. Define \(F(\theta):=\{x\in K(\theta):h_{i,\theta}(x)\geq0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,r\}\) and \(v(\theta):=\inf_{x\in F(\theta)}f_\theta(x)\), using \(+\infty\) for an empty fiber. The joint problem decomposes exactly as \[\inf\{f_\theta(x):\theta\in P,\ x\in F(\theta)\}=\inf_{\theta\in P}v(\theta).\] Any attained minimizer of the right-hand side, paired with an attained fiber minimizer, solves the joint problem globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing the parameter produces conditional subproblems whose value function can be minimized to recover the exact joint optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{\theta\in P,\ x\in F(\theta)}f_\theta(x)=\inf_{\theta\in P}v(\theta)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear scalarization certificate for monotone strictly quasiconcave composite minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of a polar-cone linear scalarization all of whose optimizers solve a composite global minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, strictly quasiconcave, and \(K\)-monotonic on a closed convex set \(Y\subset\mathbb R^q\). Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^q\) be a polyhedral convex cone satisfying \(K\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(Y)\), and let \(g:D\to\mathbb R^q\) satisfy \(g(D)\subset\operatorname{int}Y\). If \(F\circ g\) attains a minimum on \(D\), then there exists \(t\in-K^\circ\) such that
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}\langle t,g(x)\rangle
\subseteq
\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}F(g(x)).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If F is continuous, strictly quasiconcave, and K-monotonic on the closed convex set Y; K is a polyhedral convex cone contained in the recession cone of Y; g(D) lies in the interior of Y; and the composite minimum is attained, then some parameter t in −K° defines a linear scalarization whose every optimizer also minimizes F composed with g.
assumptions_latex: F:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R\text{ is continuous, strictly quasiconcave, and }K\text{-monotonic on }Y
Y\subset\mathbb R^q\text{ is closed and convex}
K\subset\mathbb R^q\text{ is a polyhedral convex cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists t\in-K^\circ:\quad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}\langle t,g(x)\rangle\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}F(g(x))

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-System Characterization of a Parametric Cell
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of each cell by threshold maps and pairwise linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A cell \(\Pi\) is characterized by a map \(k_\Pi:I_*^2\to\{1,\ldots,m,m+1\}\) and is the solution set of
\[
t_{i_1}+c_{i_1j}\le t_2+c_{i_2j}\quad\forall(i_1,i_2)\in I_*^2\text{ such that }v_{i_1,i_2}(j)\ge k_\Pi(i_1,i_2),
\]
\[
t_{i_1}+c_{i_1j}\ge t_2+c_{i_2j}\quad\forall(i_1,i_2)\in I_*^2\text{ such that }v_{i_1,i_2}(j)<k_\Pi(i_1,i_2).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each cell Pi is characterized by a threshold map k_Pi on ordered index pairs and equals the solution set of the corresponding pairwise linear inequalities, with the inequality direction determined by whether v is at least the threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi=\left\{t:\begin{array}{l}t_{i_1}+c_{i_1j}\le t_2+c_{i_2j}\text{ if }v_{i_1,i_2}(j)\ge k_\Pi(i_1,i_2),\\ t_{i_1}+c_{i_1j}\ge t_2+c_{i_2j}\text{ if }v_{i_1,i_2}(j)<k_\Pi(i_1,i_2),\quad\forall(i_1,i_2)\in I_*^2\end{array}\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: PA algorithm for the reverse-convex master problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral approximation algorithm using vertex-indexed linear programs, incumbent improvement, and parameter-polytope cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a vertex \(x^0\in D\) with \(h(x^0)>0\), translate \(D\) and \(C\) by \(-x^0\), initialize an incumbent \(\bar x^1\) with value \(\gamma_1=\langle c,\bar x^1\rangle\) (or \(\gamma_1=+\infty\) if none exists), and initialize the parameter polytope with vertex set \(V_1\). At iteration \(k\), for each relevant \(t\in V_k\), solve \[\mu(t)=\max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^r t_i\langle c^i,x\rangle\mid x\in D,\ \langle c,x\rangle\le\gamma_k\right\}.\] If \(\mu(t)\le1\) for all \(t\in V_k\), terminate with \(\bar x^k\) optimal when \(\gamma_k<\infty\), and declare infeasibility otherwise. If some \(\mu(t^k)>1\), take a basic optimal solution \(x^k\). When \(x^k\notin C\), locally improve it, update the incumbent and \(\gamma_k\), and repeat. When \(x^k\in C\), set \(\theta_k=\sup\{\theta\mid\theta x^k\in C\}\), retain the incumbent, and refine the parameter polytope by \[\widetilde P_{k+1}=\widetilde P_k\cap\left\{t\mid\sum_{i=1}^r t_i\langle x^k,c^i\rangle\le\frac1{\theta_k}\right\};\] compute its new vertex set and continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The PA algorithm starts from a translated reverse-convex model and an optional incumbent. It solves a linear program for each current parameter-polytope vertex. If every resulting value is at most one, it certifies either incumbent optimality or infeasibility. Otherwise it either improves a newly found feasible candidate or cuts the parameter polytope using the radial boundary point of C and repeats.
assumptions_latex: x^0\text{ is a vertex of }D\text{ with }h(x^0)>0
\widetilde P_1\text{ is the initial simplex-based parameter polytope with vertex set }V_1
\gamma_1=\langle c,\bar x^1\rangle\text{ for an available feasible incumbent, or }+\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\forall t\in V_k,\ \mu(t)\le1\bigr]\Rightarrow\begin{cases}\bar x^k\text{ is optimal},&\gamma_k<\infty,\\(MRP)\text{ is infeasible},&\gamma_k=+\infty;\end{cases}\quad\text{otherwise the incumbent is improved or }\widetilde P_k\text{ is cut and the iteration continues.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rectangular branch-and-bound algorithm for GPTP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incumbent-based pruning and relaxation-gap branching for (GPTP).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start from a rectangle \(M_1\subset Y\), a feasible incumbent \(y^1\), and \(\mathrm{INV}=\varphi(y^1)\). For every active rectangle \(M\), solve \(\mathrm{CP}(M)\) to obtain its lower bound \(\beta(M)\) and relaxation solution \((\bar x(M),\bar y(M),\bar z(M))\); update the incumbent and discard every \(M\) with \(\beta(M)\ge\mathrm{INV}-\varepsilon\). If no rectangle remains, the incumbent is globally \(\varepsilon\)-optimal. Otherwise select a rectangle minimizing \(\beta(M)\), choose \(i_k\in\arg\max_i\{g_i(\bar y_i^k)-l_{i,M_k}(\bar y_i^k)\}\), and either terminate globally when the maximal gap is zero or subdivide \(M_k\) through \((\bar y^k,i_k)\) and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve the convex relaxation on every active rectangle, update the best feasible objective, prune rectangles whose lower bounds cannot improve it by more than epsilon, and branch on a coordinate having maximal concave-envelope gap. Exhaustion certifies global epsilon-optimality, while a zero maximal gap certifies global optimality.
assumptions_latex: \beta(M)\text{ is the optimal value of the associated convex relaxation }\mathrm{CP}(M)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal R_k=\varnothing\Rightarrow y^k\text{ is globally }\varepsilon\text{-optimal};\qquad \max_i\{g_i(\bar y_i^k)-l_{i,M_k}(\bar y_i^k)\}=0\Rightarrow\bar y^k\text{ is globally optimal.}

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Outer Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cutting-plane outer approximation of a compactly restricted Lagrangian dual hypograph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_{z\in C}\{f(z):h_i(z)\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,r\}\), define \(L(z,\lambda):=f(z)-\lambda^{\mathsf T}h(z)\) and \(q(\lambda):=\inf_{z\in C}L(z,\lambda)\). Choose a compact multiplier set \(\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R_+^r\), an initial finite set \(Z_0\subset C\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). At iteration \(k\), solve \[\max_{\lambda\in\Lambda,t}\{t:t\leq L(z,\lambda)\text{ for every }z\in Z_k\}\] to obtain \((\lambda^k,t^k)\), compute \(z^k\in\arg\min_{z\in C}L(z,\lambda^k)\), and stop when \(t^k-L(z^k,\lambda^k)\leq\varepsilon\); otherwise set \(Z_{k+1}:=Z_k\cup\{z^k\}\). The returned multiplier is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal for the restricted dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A master problem bounds the dual value using sampled Lagrangian cuts; an exact inner oracle adds a violated cut until the dual gap is within tolerance.
assumptions_latex: The inner minimization oracle is exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq t^k-q(\lambda^k)\leq\varepsilon\) at termination.

notation.meaning: master upper estimate of the dual value

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual outer approximation for network-constrained parametric decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Master-polytope refinement for (SCP) using a dual inequality from a fixed-parameter linear subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(P_1=Y\times[\alpha,\beta]\), where \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are lower and upper bounds on \(\langle c,x\rangle\) over \(\{x\mid Bx=d,\ x\ge0\}\). Given \(P_k\) containing every \((y,t)\) admitting an \(x\ge0\) satisfying (9.96), choose \((y^k,t^k)\in\operatorname{argmin}\{t+g(y)\mid(y,t)\in P_k\}\). Solve \(\min\{\langle c,x\rangle\mid Qx=y^k,\ Bx=d,\ x\ge0\}\) and its dual \(\max\{\langle y^k,u\rangle+\langle d,v\rangle\mid Q^Tu+B^Tv\le c\}\). If \(\langle c,x^k\rangle\le t^k\), terminate with \((x^k,y^k)\); otherwise set \(P_{k+1}=P_k\cap\{(y,t)\mid\langle y,u^k\rangle+\langle d,v^k\rangle\le t\}\) and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize the master objective over the current outer polytope, solve the fixed-parameter primal and dual linear programs, and either terminate with an SCP solution or add the resulting dual inequality. In the stated PTP and MCCNFP specializations, the primal subproblem is respectively a transportation problem or a minimum-cost network-flow problem.
assumptions_latex: P_k\subseteq P_1\text{ contains every }(y,t)\text{ for which some }x\ge0\text{ satisfies (9.96)}
x^k\text{ and }(u^k,v^k)\text{ are optimal solutions of the displayed primal-dual pair}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle c,x^k\rangle\le t^k\Rightarrow(x^k,y^k)\text{ solves (SCP)};\qquad \langle c,x^k\rangle>t^k\Rightarrow P_{k+1}=P_k\cap\{(y,t):\langle y,u^k\rangle+\langle d,v^k\rangle\le t\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Disconnected Feasible Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single convex exclusion can disconnect an otherwise convex host.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the convex host be \(C=[-2,2]\), and impose the reverse-convex constraint \(g(x):=x^2-1\geq0\). Although \(g\) is convex on \(C\), the feasible set is \[F=\{x\in C:g(x)\geq0\}=[-2,-1]\cup[1,2].\] Thus one reverse-convex inequality can produce two disjoint feasible components. Consequently, connectedness of the convex host does not imply connectedness of the reverse-convex feasible region, and a local search confined to one component need not inspect the other component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Excluding the open interval where a convex quadratic is negative splits a convex interval into two disconnected feasible components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in C:g(x)\geq0\}=[-2,-1]\cup[1,2]\) is disconnected.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constructed example and its disconnected feasible set are correct, and counterexample is the appropriate knowledge kind. No citation or explicit standard-field rationale supports the record.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Exclusion Combinatorial Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An explicit separable family realizes exponential growth in feasible components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(m\geq1\) and \(0<\delta<1/2\). On the convex host \(C=[0,1]^m\), impose \(m\) reverse-convex inequalities \[g_i(x):=(x_i-1/2)^2-\delta^2\geq0,\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.\] Each \(g_i\) is convex, and the feasible set equals the Cartesian product \[F=\prod_{i=1}^m\bigl([0,1/2-\delta]\cup[1/2+\delta,1]\bigr).\] Hence \(F\) has exactly \(2^m\) pairwise disjoint, full-dimensional box components. Any exact component-enumeration method therefore requires at least \(2^m\) component outputs on this family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent convex exclusions in each coordinate create exactly two choices per coordinate and therefore exponentially many feasible boxes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) has exactly \(2^m\) connected components.

notation.meaning: half-width of each excluded coordinate interval

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The separable construction correctly has exactly 2^m connected full-dimensional box components and gives an output-size lower bound for component enumeration. No citation or explicit standard-field rationale is supplied.

children.title: Reverse-Convex Boundary Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Degenerate geometric structure on reverse-convex solution boundaries.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-Subgradient Redundancy Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp criterion for an algebraically active but geometrically vacuous reverse-convex zero level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(g:U\to\mathbb R\) be convex. If \(g(\bar x)=0\) and \(0\in\partial g(\bar x)\), then \(g(y)\geq0\) for every \(y\in U\). Hence \(\{y\in U:g(y)<0\}=\varnothing\), the reverse-convex inequality is redundant on \(U\), and \(\bar x\) is not incident to a nonempty exclusion boundary. Equivalently, if \(\{g<0\}\ne\varnothing\), then \(0\notin\partial g(x)\) at every zero-level point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero subgradient at a zero-level point forces the convex exclusion to be empty, so algebraic activity there is not genuine boundary geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{y\in U:g(y)<0\}=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential at the active point
strict convex exclusion induced by g

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Subgradient Redundancy Criterion
Reverse-Convex Boundary Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic activity with a vanishing gradient need not describe a regular feasible boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in[-1,1]}x^2\) subject to the reverse-convex inequality \(g(x):=x^2\geq0\). The unique minimizer is \(x^*=0\), where \(g(x^*)=0\) and \(g'(x^*)=0\). Moreover, \(g(x)\geq0\) holds throughout the host, so \(x^*\) is not on the relative topological boundary of the feasible set. The first-order linearization at \(x^*\) is the vacuous inequality \(0\geq0\). Thus algebraic activity alone does not provide a regular reverse-convex boundary or a nonzero supporting normal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reverse-convex constraint can be algebraically active with zero gradient while remaining locally redundant, so its zero level set does not furnish a regular feasible boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*=0\), \(g(x^*)=g'(x^*)=0\), and \(x^*\notin\operatorname{relbd}\{x\in C:g(x)\geq0\}\).

children.title: Nonisolated Reverse-Convex Solutions
children.top_down_role: Solution sets containing continua or locally indistinguishable optima.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Isolated and Nonisolated Global Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological classification of global minimizers within a reverse-convex solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S^*=\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\). A point \(x^*\in S^*\) is isolated if some \(\varepsilon>0\) satisfies \(S^*\cap B_\varepsilon(x^*)=\{x^*\}\). It is nonisolated if every \(\varepsilon>0\) satisfies \((S^*\setminus\{x^*\})\cap B_\varepsilon(x^*)\ne\varnothing\). Thus nonisolatedness means accumulation by other global solutions, not merely the existence of several separated minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global solution is nonisolated exactly when other global solutions occur arbitrarily close to it; separated multiplicity alone is insufficient.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a reverse-convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ is nonisolated}\iff \forall\varepsilon>0,\ (S^*\setminus\{x^*\})\cap B_\varepsilon(x^*)\ne\varnothing.

notation.meaning: open Euclidean ball about the solution

knowledge_statements.title: Isolated and Nonisolated Global Solutions
Nonisolated Reverse-Convex Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A reverse-convex program can have continua of global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(C=[-1,1]^2\), minimize \(f(x)=x_2^2\) subject to the convex exclusion inequality \(g(x):=x_1^2-1/4\geq0\). The feasible set is the union of two closed strips. Its global optimal value is \(0\), and the solution set is \[S^*=\bigl([-1,-1/2]\cup[1/2,1]\bigr)\times\{0\}.\] Every point of \(S^*\) is a global minimizer and none is isolated within \(S^*\). Hence finiteness or isolatedness of reverse-convex solutions requires additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic objective constant along feasible strips yields two line segments of global minimizers rather than isolated solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^*=([-1,-1/2]\cup[1/2,1])\times\{0\}\) is nonisolated.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feasible and optimal sets are computed correctly, and the example establishes nonisolated global solutions. No citation or explicit standard-field rationale is supplied.

children.title: Degenerate Solution Manifolds
children.top_down_role: Nonisolated solution structures supported by degenerate boundaries.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degenerate Solution Manifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Opposing host and reverse-convex boundaries can support a positive-dimensional, tangentially flat optimal manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\geq2\), \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_2\leq1\}\), impose \(g(x):=\|x\|_2^2-1\geq0\), and minimize \(f(x)=0\). The host inequality and reverse-convex inequality together give \(S^*=\{x:\|x\|_2=1\}\). Thus the feasible and optimal set is an \((n-1)\)-dimensional manifold. The objective is flat in every tangent direction, so optimizer isolation, positive tangential curvature, and finite-candidate conclusions fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opposing ball constraints leave the sphere, and a constant objective makes that entire positive-dimensional manifold globally optimal and tangentially flat.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S^*=\{x:\|x\|_2=1\}\text{ is an }(n-1)\text{-dimensional global-solution manifold}.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Solution Manifolds

children.title: Boundary-Localization Failure
children.top_down_role: Limits of localization mechanisms near degenerate or nonisolated solutions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary-Localization Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Without hypotheses excluding flat interior optima, global optimizers need not lie on exclusion boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=[-2,2]\), impose the reverse-convex inequality \(g(x):=x^2-1\geq0\), and minimize \(f(x)=0\). Every feasible point is globally optimal. In particular, \(x=3/2\) is optimal and satisfies \(g(3/2)=5/4>0\), so it is not on the exclusion boundary \(g(x)=0\). Hence a universal claim that every optimizer lies on an active exclusion boundary is false without additional objective hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant objective makes strictly feasible points optimal, disproving unconditional localization of every optimizer to an exclusion boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x=3/2\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C,\ g(x)\geq0}f(x),\qquad g(3/2)>0.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Localization Failure
Unbounded Convex Hosts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dropping compactness can destroy existence and finite lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take the unbounded convex host \(C=\mathbb R\), impose the reverse-convex inequality \(g(x):=x^2-1\geq0\), and minimize \(f(x)=-x\). The feasible set is \(( -\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\). Along the feasible sequence \(x_k=k\), one has \(f(x_k)=-k\to-\infty\). Hence the problem is unbounded below and has no global minimizer. Compact-host existence arguments and algorithms requiring bounded polyhedral enumeration cannot be transferred to unbounded hosts without coercivity, level-boundedness, or explicit valid bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an unbounded host, a reverse-convex feasible ray can let the objective diverge to minus infinity, so no global minimizer exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf\{f(x):x\in C,\ g(x)\geq0\}=-\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Level-Boundedness Restores Attainment on an Unbounded Host
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient replacement for compact-host assumptions in reverse-convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(f:F\to\mathbb R\) be lower semicontinuous. If \(f\) is level-bounded on \(F\), meaning that \(\{x\in F:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is bounded for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), then \(f\) attains a finite global minimum on \(F\), even when the convex host containing \(F\) is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed feasibility, lower semicontinuity, and level-boundedness restore finite attainment even on an unbounded host.
assumptions_latex: For every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), \(\{x\in F:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\ne\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad\min_{x\in F}f(x)\in\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: objective sublevel set relative to F

children.title: Generalized Geometric-Signomial Program Family
children.top_down_role: Classical positive-variable multiplicative models, from convexifiable geometric-programming subclasses to nonconvex generalized geometric and signomial programs, with family-specific transformations, relaxations, partitioning, convergence, and computational interfaces.

children.title: Geometric-Signomial Model Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Convexifiable subclasses are retained as prerequisites and boundaries; the nonconvex generalized families remain the principal subject.

knowledge_statements.title: Monomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-variable monomials used in geometric programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A monomial on the positive orthant \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\) is a function \[m(x)=c\prod_{j=1}^n x_j^{a_j},\] where \(c>0\) and the exponents \(a_j\in\mathbb R\) are arbitrary real numbers. Under the logarithmic substitution \(y_j=\log x_j\), its logarithm is affine: \[\log m(e^y)=\log c+a^{\mathsf T}y.\] Consequently, an equality between two monomials becomes an affine equality in logarithmic variables, and a monomial inequality can be normalized and represented by an affine logarithmic inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive coefficient times arbitrary real powers of positive variables is a monomial; taking logarithms converts it to an affine function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\log m(e^y)=\log c+a^{\mathsf T}y\).

source_refs.locator: 3.5.2 Model Variants and Solution Approaches p. 193

source_witnesses.locator: 3.5.2 Model Variants and Solution Approaches p. 193

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Log-Affinity Does Not Imply Ordinary Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between geometric log-space structure and convexity in the original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A geometric-programming monomial need not be convex in its original positive variables. For example, \(m(x)=x^{1/2}\) on \(\mathbb R_{++}\) satisfies \(\log m(e^y)=y/2\), while \(m''(x)=-1/(4x^{3/2})<0\), so it is strictly concave. Thus monomial log-affinity cannot be replaced by ordinary convexity in \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Monomials are log-affine but need not be convex in their original variables; the square-root monomial is strictly concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Log-affinity of a monomial does not imply convexity in the original coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Affinity Does Not Imply Ordinary Convexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algebraic Closure of Positive Monomials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure rules for geometric-programming monomials on the positive orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m_1(x)=c_1x^a\) and \(m_2(x)=c_2x^b\) be monomials on \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\), with \(c_1,c_2>0\), and let \(r\in\mathbb R\). Then
\[m_1m_2=(c_1c_2)x^{a+b},\qquad \frac{m_1}{m_2}=\frac{c_1}{c_2}x^{a-b},\qquad m_1^r=c_1^r x^{ra}\]
are monomials. Consequently every finite product, ratio, or real power of positive monomials remains log-affine after \(y=\log x\). A sum of two nonproportional monomials is generally a posynomial rather than a monomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive monomials are closed under products, ratios, and real powers, but generally not under addition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Products, ratios, and real powers preserve the monomial class and log-affinity.
knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Closure of Positive Monomials
Posynomial Geometric Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form geometric programs and their logarithmic convex reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A standard posynomial geometric program minimizes a posynomial \(f_0(x)\) over \(x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), subject to \(f_i(x)\leq1\) for posynomials \(f_i\) and \(m_j(x)=1\) for monomials \(m_j\). Write \(x=e^y\). Each transformed inequality is \[\log f_i(e^y)=\log\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K_i}\exp(a_{ik}^{\mathsf T}y+b_{ik})\right)\leq0,\] which is convex in \(y\), while each monomial equality becomes affine. Minimizing \(f_0\) is equivalently minimizing \(\log f_0(e^y)\); hence the transformed problem is a convex optimization problem with the same minimizers under \(x=e^y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Logarithmic variables turn posynomial inequalities into log-sum-exp constraints and monomial equalities into affine constraints, yielding an equivalent convex problem.
assumptions_latex: All posynomial coefficients are strictly positive.
All monomial equality coefficients are strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=e^y\) gives an equivalent convex formulation in \(y\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Posynomial Closure and Division Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic closure properties distinguishing posynomials from complementary ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(p\) and \(q\) are posynomials on \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\), \(m\) is a monomial, and \(\alpha>0\), then \(p+q\), \(\alpha p\), \(pq\), and \(p/m\) are posynomials. In contrast, \(p/q\) need not be a posynomial when \(q\) is not a monomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Posynomials are closed under addition, positive scaling, multiplication, and division by monomials, but not under general posynomial division.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p+q,\ \alpha p,\ pq,\ p/m\text{ are posynomials, while }p/q\text{ need not be}.
knowledge_statements.title: Posynomial Closure and Division Boundary
